subtopic: CONTRIBUTIONS TO CONTINUATION OF PEACE KEEPING FORCE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CONTRIBUTIONS TO CONTINUATION OF PEACE KEEPING FORCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether a contribution is going to be made by the other nations within the United Nations in connection with Canada's further participation in the Cyprus force for an additional period of time. As I understand it, Canada and the United Kingdom are the only two nations which are making their contributions fully and voluntarily. What is being done in this connection to ensure, to put it mildly, that Canada is not a kind of Santa Claus in these peace keeping operations?

subtopic: CONTRIBUTIONS TO CONTINUATION OF PEACE KEEPING FORCE
speechtext:
Voluntary contributions
have been made by a number of states, notably by the United Kingdom and the United States. Canada is not the only country which has undertaken to pay her own expenses. Ireland is in that category. With regard to the three month period, both Canada and Ireland have taken the position that if the financial situation in the United Nations should become such that reimbursement could take place, we would expect that there should be reimbursement.
speakername: Hon. Paul  Marlin@Secretary of Slate for External Affairs

subtopic: CONTRIBUTIONS TO CONTINUATION OF PEACE KEEPING FORCE
speechtext: Would the minister say what other nation is contributing its force and paying the cost of that force, other than the United Kingdom?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTRIBUTIONS TO CONTINUATION OF PEACE KEEPING FORCE
speechtext: I said that in addition there were Ireland and Canada. Other countries are receiving assistance out of the voluntary fund.

subtopic: CONTRIBUTIONS TO CONTINUATION OF PEACE KEEPING FORCE
speechtext: Was there any particular reason why Canada should have been placed in this beneficent position?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTRIBUTIONS TO CONTINUATION OF PEACE KEEPING FORCE
speechtext:
Well, if we had not taken this position, in the first place
I am sure there might not have been a United Nations force. In addition, we felt the fact that we had to pay for the air lift both going and coming must and should be regarded as a contribution, as well, to the voluntary fund.

subtopic: CONTRIBUTIONS TO CONTINUATION OF PEACE KEEPING FORCE
speechtext: The argument the minister makes is accepted, but it does not apply to the second period, the additional period. What has been done in recent weeks to assure that other nations will provide the necessary funds, or at least a portion of the funds, to meet the cost of the Canadian force there?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTRIBUTIONS TO CONTINUATION OF PEACE KEEPING FORCE
speechtext:
As I said, in the first three months assistance was given by the United States and some other countries, providing enough money to pay for the operation of the force; subject, of course, to the undertakings and commitments made by Canada, Ireland and, as the right hon. gentleman says, the United Kingdom.
With regard to the second three month period, there have been further contributions made by a number of the original contributing states. When the question of a renewal of the mandate was considered the financial aspect of the problem was examined, and it would not have been possible for a renewal to take place if the participating countries had not proceeded on the basis established previously.
As I stated in this house, it is regrettable that other states in the United Nations have not recognized their obligations under the charter and made the contributions which membership in the organization involves. However, because other countries have refused to live up to their obligations, that is no reason, as I am sure the right hon. gentleman would agree, why Canada should be delinquent with regard to its commitment.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON GRANTS TO FAIRS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON GRANTS TO FAIRS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to address a question to the Minister of Agriculture and ask him whether he would dispel the fears of the Ontario association of agricultural societies by assuring them that the government has no intention of completely cancelling out the grants to class A and class B fairs, which have been suspended for a period of two years.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harry W. Hays (Minisler of Agriculture):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON GRANTS TO FAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been in consultation with the executive of the A fairs in this connection; I have also discussed grants with the B fairs executive. I will be meeting them again in the not too far distant future. We have some plans that we would like to discuss with them. We have at the moment a pilot project in so far as livestock exhibits are

concerned, basing them on utility values; and we also have some plans which we think will do an even better job than the old grants did for the fairs since 1947, and which have now been suspended since 1962.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON GRANTS TO FAIRS
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Could the Minister of Agriculture state whether the capital grants will be continued to the A and B fairs?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON GRANTS TO FAIRS
speechtext: I suggested to them at the time we were running this pilot project that as soon as it was completed, after the London exhibition, we would like to have the executives of both the B fairs and the A fairs and the exhibitors see us and we would discuss the whole program of grants, prize money, and so on, in so far as exhibitions are concerned. Until such time as this project has been completed, no grants will be considered.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON GRANTS TO FAIRS
speechtext: I should like to direct a supplementary question to the Minister of Agriculture with regard to the fall fairs. Does he not think it is a little late for the government to formulate a policy with respect to this important item?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON GRANTS TO FAIRS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I suppose the hon. gentleman is referring to the capital grants which have been suspended, as the hon. member knows, since June of 1962. We have honoured the $3,000 per year for fairs, and there has been no change there. There are many requests for capital grants, but we think with the program we are planning now, if the pilot project is successful, we will be able to do something that the 128 exhibitions in Canada have long needed. We think these fairs are no longer just agricultural societies for agricultural purposes but they are cultural centres. Many of these smaller fairs are asking for $30,000 when they should get $200,000, and that is what we are thinking of.

Order, please. I should like to call to the attention of hon. members that the question period has now lasted 64 minutes. I am wondering whether we could not get on with the business before the house.
I thank the Minister of Forestry for the information he has given us. There has been so much activity in the house that his appointment passed unnoticed.

I wish to protest against the words of the hon. member. I am convinced that he does not mean what he said.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Tuesday, July 7, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Gordon-Mr. Lamoureux in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the revision of certain fiscal arrangements with the provinces and to provide adjustments of fiscal arrangements and taxation provisions consequential upon the provision of youth allowances to parents resident in certain provinces.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in speaking on this resolution I intend to traverse generally the position of dominion-provincial relations in recent years, to deal with the various courses of action that were taken to meet the needs of the provinces to an ever increasing extent and, before I conclude, to make certain suggestions relative to courses of action which we in the opposition believe should be taken.
I commence by referring to the expeditious way in which legislation has received the attention of the house during the last few days. Indeed, this has been the first opportunity the house has had to deal with legislative matters or resolutions necessary for the welfare of the country, and you will have noticed in this regard, Mr. Chairman, that in every way the opposition, joining in the need for examination and maintaining its rights to scrutinize carefully and criticize where necessary, has expeditiously given passage to these measures.
It is of more than passing interest that the government has revealed itself again today as not having its legislative program ready despite the fact that many of these matters were included in the speech from the throne. With the possible exception of the flag question, which only in the month of June became one of transcendent importance, these other matters have been before the government since February; yet we find today that a matter as important as loans to students, which was one of those things which were to receive attention during those momentous 60 days of decision, is not yet ready. Furthermore, we learned that while we gave passage to the defence bill following careful examination, as well as one or two other matters of legislation, the government, which enjoys an overwhelming majority in the other place, has not seen fit to have the other place sitting so these matters, major in the viewpoint of the government, would not be delayed.
Federal-Provincial Relations
All of this is indicative of a state of mind. Events of recent days, not excluding the resolution now before the house, are indicative of a determination on the part of the government to have an election at an early date. These questions are brought up, but ever and anon we are informed that over us, as a portent of the possibility of a vacation, hangs the sword of Damocles, if I may borrow that allusion, should we fail to do what the government wants. Measures such as redistribution are left in cold storage. This is all most interesting; and when we realize something of the degree to which the press favourable to the government keeps referring to the opposition denying the passage of legislation, it all looks to me like an excuse in anticipation.
This resolution is important. It represents a further step in the field of dominion-provincial relations. Its design and purpose, I take it, are to bring to our country a greater degree of unity. I think all of us as Canadians are most anxious to do all we can to bring about unity within our country. Yet it is passing strange that three years before Canada will celebrate the one hundredth anniversary of confederation too few Canadians have knowledge of the history and the traditions of this country, of the meaning of the federal system. Only the other day it came to my notice that while in other countries those who were the fathers of their countries are remembered and recalled, few Canadians, even in this house, would be able to name more than a few fathers of confederation if asked to do so. I am not placing myself in any higher category, but if we had an i.q. test in this connection I do not think the House of Commons would be able to achieve a higher degree of favourable marks than the average Canadian.
Strange it seems that we in our country do not look at our past and our traditions. Strange it seems that when one looks at the Canadian Almanac, the Parliamentary Guide, the Canada Year Book and the Encyclopaedia Britannica there is no reference in any of them to the names and the persons of the fathers of confederation. I hope that in so far as the parliamentary red book is concerned, that will be rectified, and in any other publications of the government of Canada. It shows on our part a lack of appreciation of the spiritual values of our nation. I entered into a competition with myself in this regard to name the fathers of confederation, and I did not get too far along the road after I had brought to mind those who from time
5248	HOUSE OF
Federal-Provincial Relations to time receive consistent reference. All of this indicates the need of something being done to bring about a strengthening of our confederation through knowledge and through an appreciation of history.
The resolution placed before the house by the minister is one that I am sure will receive close examination. It is of interest to note that the minister in his palmy days of authoring dreamed of the day when deficits would be no more, when the halcyon days of Liberalism would return, to use his own words, and deficits would be at an end. Since the Minister of Finance has been in office we know now that deficits can be respectable, deficits can be worthy of commendation, provided they represent deficits incurred by a government of which one is a member.
The minister is in this position; that on the basis of the lost revenue consequent on this resolution being passed and the legislation based thereon translated into law, he must act. In the United States taxes are being cut and the economy is being advanced and accelerated. We in Canada, following the acceleration in the United States have, in the backwash, necessarily been carried along as a result of the expansion in the economy there. The minister must inevitably, whenever he brings in another budget, increase taxation in Canada. Income taxation is bound to go up. This is another reason why the government is looking for an excuse for an election. Being a diplomatic group, they do not want to do anything that might cause ill feeling in this nation.
A moment ago, sir, I mentioned the economy in the United States. I read from the New York Times of June 28:
Economy of the United States sets a record for first half. Boom continues through its fortieth month for longest peacetime surge since world war II.
We said the boom was under way when they were in opposition, and those who sit on the treasury benches today said there was no boom. Now they admit we are in the fortieth boom month in Canada; the minister himself admitted that. In the United States, however, it is predicted that there will be clear sailing for another nine months and thereafter no one can predict. All these things, taken together with the attitude of this government from day to day, indicate that if they can gallop without appearing to do so, to hold an election, they will do just that, and endeavour to blame the opposition.
I again emphasize this. Bring on your legislation. Just as an aside I may say that the Minister of Agriculture and those associated


with him in the first 60 days were going to give milk to all the school children in Canada. Where has it gone? Where has that promise gone? It is just another one. They promised 10,000 scholarships. Where are those scholarships? They would make an idea attractive for another election. Even an hon. member like the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who is completely removed from political considerations at all times, would see the advantages in this, the possible use of the same promise twice. This is a cynical attitude taken by some, but not those on this side of the house.
Now, sir, what about these fiscal arrangements? Well, it is of interest to follow them. The course in this regard has been equally uncertain as in so many other cases. They advanced their ideas. Several federal-provincial conferences were held. The premiers gathered. Naturally they wanted a larger share of the tax dollar because they could not discharge their responsibilities under the constitutional distribution of powers. They did not get very much until things started to move. One or the other of the premiers said that action was going to be taken. At the last federal-provincial conference there was set up a committee for an in-depth examination of our general fiscal situation as between the federal government and the provinces.
Then the criticism came. The government decided not to wait for the expert advice they would have received in that connection. The first two conferences indicated a lack of imagination since this government came into office; a lack of preparation and a lack of purpose; changing goals in mid conference and a lack of definite proposals so there had not been sufficient preliminary study. There was uncertainty; one day on and another day off. Finally, after this year's conference, there was strong criticism of the government of Canada. Then, suddenly, there was recognition by the government that some action should be taken.
When we came into office we said we would assure the provinces a larger share of the tax dollar, and we did so. I intend to refer to that in particular. The necessity for this resulted from the fact that the previous government had failed to discharge its responsibilities to the provinces. They had left Canada in such confusion and annoyance, that even those who ordinarily were members of the Liberal fold were critical.
I think of the tradition of the Atlantic provinces before we came into office in 1957. The hon. member for Victoria-Carleton was

premier of New Brunswick. He saw the situation there. He took strong objection to the lack of action. Someone might say he was prejudiced. Well, what did the premier of Newfoundland say? On June 25, 1955, when speaking at St. Andrews-by-the-Sea, he threatened-that is Premier Joseph Smallwood-to lead Newfoundland out of confederation unless the federal government stopped discriminating against the four Atlantic provinces, including his own. Even he could not stomach the failure of the government to act. He said this:
Before we become second class citizens of Canada we will show the other maritime provinces how to get out of confederation.
This is very much like what is being said today about the union jack, sir; a second flag for Canada, which is what Mr. Smallwood demanded. Then I should like to bring this to the attention of the non-political members sitting opposite:
The federal government has made miserable proposals-
This was the government of Mr. St. Laurent.
-of sharing the cost in surveys of the wealth of timber, hydro power and minerals. We have gone ahead on our own and since confederation have spent $23 million to help build new industries.
If conferation was not to recognize the right of all Canadians to some equality in living standards and opportunity, Newfoundland and the maritimes might as well be declared game preserves for the holidays of Canadians from more prosperous provinces.
I am sure the Minister of Justice has not heard that before. It is an amazing revelation from a sycophant of Liberalism. That was the position. Furthermore he said-and you understand, Mr. Chairman, I dislike placing these words on the record but I have to do it in order to establish the position of affairs when we came into office:
I am ashamed and angry to say it, but the altogether stupid, bungling, inadequate effort of great Canada to assist the Atlantic fishing industry, (which is potentially almost as valuable in dollars and cents and much more valuable in numbers of families that can be supported than the oil industry of Alberta) is a reproach to a great and progressive country.
I could go on and quote further statements on his part, but I am simply pointing out the generalizations in a statement from a completely unprejudiced source so far as the Liberal party was concerned, as to the serious state of Canadian confederation when we assumed office.
We acted immediately. There was an agreement in effect, beginning April 1, 1957 which
Federal-Provincial Relations would have continued for a period of five years. It had been signed and agreed to by all the provinces. We said it was unfair, that the 10 per cent share of personal income tax that was made available to the provinces was insufficient, and we brought in legislation to increase that share from 10 per cent to 13 per cent.
We gave proof of recognition of the financial problems resting on municipalities, by greatly increasing conditional and unconditional payments and abatements during our period of office, and I am going to refer to the record of the federal-provincial conference of 1963 in that connection. We maintained the equalization principle and made it more equitable. I recall so well that during the last election, and in 1962, the Liberal party said it would bring about equalization on the basis of the highest province. It is another of the promises made recklessly which it has failed to follow.
Here is what another author, now on the front bench of the Liberal government, had to say, and I refer to the Minister of Transport in the book entitled "The Liberal Party." At page 125 he says this:
At the national Liberal convention of 1958 the party pledged itself to alter the basis of equalization payments so that the revenues of all provinces from income taxes and succession duties would be brought up to the level of the province having the highest per capita revenue. This principle was reaffirmed at the national Liberal rally in 1961. Actually the difference in equalization payments between taking the highest province and taking the top two provinces as a standard is not very great but it is felt that basing payments on the highest province is sounder in principle.
The Prime Minister also made a similar statement. Over and over again that was basic, but in the resolution now before us that principle is permanently put in cold storage and completely evaded.
The equalization plan set out in this resolution is unfair to provinces with above average resources. That matter will be dealt with by other hon. members. We made it possible for the provinces to impose their own income tax with the federal government collecting it without charge. We took into consideration fiscal needs of the Atlantic provinces and made provision for grants of $25 million per year, later increased to $35 million per year. We did these things in order to strengthen the basic principles of confederation, to assure the maintenance of the federal system, and the independence of provincial governments.
I am now going to refer to the results of that action on our part. I am going to refer to the changes that took place and the tremendous degree to which we added to the

Federal-Provincial Relations financial resources of the provinces in so many fields. I reiterate what I have said before, that if we had not increased the share of the provinces-if we had carried out the agreement of 1957, beginning on April 1 that year, as prepared by the previous Liberal government and accepted by the provinces-[DOT] we would never have had a deficit in any year we were in office. I want to emphasize that point. Apparently the Secretary of State for External Affairs has not read the record, Otherwise the wry face he just exhibited would not have been occasioned by what I said. I suggest that he read appendix B of the federal-provincial conference of 1963 so that he will have the facts available.
I am going to ask leave of the committee to have placed on Hansard the official table so that the facts will be clearly shown relating to the summary of federal contributions to the provinces and certain payments to institutions from 1956-57 until 1962-63, because I am dealing with the period that we were in office. This is in appendix B, the official appendix to this document issued by the government of Canada; and in addition, the amounts that were paid in unconditional and conditional grants to all the provinces of Canada during the period I have mentioned, the period that we were in office and the year before. I am asking leave of the committee to place these on Hansard.

speechtext:
I am glad of that courtesy on the part of the Minister of Finance. It will, of course, be very beneficial in reducing the


length of the observations I would have to make if it were necessary to read the record in this regard.
I should like to refer to some of these fields of endeavour in which we so greatly increased the amount of federal expenditure going to the provinces. I refer to the field of vocational training. We brought about a program of vocational and technical training whose cost in 1961-62 amounted to $35,921,000 and $206 million in 1962-63. We increased greatly the amount of assistance to highways for resource development. My hon. friend from Yukon and my hon. friend from Mackenzie will recall what was done in this connection. In the field of municipal winter works, which had not previously been in existence, we spent during the last year we were in office some $27.29 million.
To summarize the increase in the amounts we made available to the provinces, unconditional grants in 1956-57 totalled $552,653 million. In 1962-63 they amounted to $991,526 million. In order to be entirely fair I also intend to give the figures for 1958 and 1959, because some changes were made just before we came to office. The amount of such payments in unconditional grants in 1958-59 was $744,622 million. In other words, even accepting those figures as applicable to the government which I had the honour to lead, the increase during our period of office in this connection alone amounted to some $228 million.
Then in the field of conditional grants- agriculture, health, hospital insurance, welfare, fitness and amateur sport and so on-* the amount paid to the provinces in 1957-58 was $144,844 million. In 1958-59 it was $248,356, and in the last year we were in office it was $842,348 million. In other words there was an increase of approximately $698 million. Add those together, and I say again, at no time would there have been a deficit but for these extra payments, one of which was in the field of hospital insurance. The previous government had placed the legislation on the statute books, but we had to finance it. That financing in 1962-63-which the previous government had nothing to worry about because all it did was to have the legislation passed-amounted to $336 million.
These are things which need to be clearly set out. When the Minister of Finance was writing his book, all this was simple. All you had to do was elect a Liberal government and all would be well financially in this nation, and deficits would be as dead as the dodo. There is no thought of that today. The

promises of 1962-63 have gone the way of milk for school children.
The statistics tell the story of what we did to achieve reasonable opportunity for the provinces. What about agricultural assistance? Assistance in this field when we came into office amounted to $938,000. It went up until in 1959-60 it amounted to $6,729,000. Then it went down to $5,174,000 in 1961-62 and to $3,279,000 in 1962-63. But there were tremendous expenditures in this connection during the intervening years in other fields such as P.F.A.A., P.F.R.A. and the like.
I believe this; that one of the major reasons behind the attitude of separatism of which one hears in this country is not a matter of political consideration but results from the failure of this government to act on behalf of eastern agriculture. Several hon. members have been pressing for action in this connection but nothing has been done to meet the problems of eastern agriculture. My hon. friend from Qu'Appelle, when he was minister of agriculture, brought about legislation to set up ARDA. I will be perfectly frank. When the plan was first placed before some of us we wondered how it could be made effective. He made it effective. This government has not acted. This government has failed to use ARDA in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec in areas where productivity is not sufficient for a fair and proper return to farmers there. And when I read the other day that 10,000 or 18,000 farmers in the province of Quebec-

speechtext: Sixteen thousand.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
All right; call it the medium figure. Whatever the number was, that many farmers could not be wrong. There is reason in what they are advocating. My hon. friend from St. Hyacinthe-Bagot has dealt with this question over and over again and placed the needs of his province before the house and the country, as has the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska and, of course, my hon. friend from Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, who has never been backward in the manner in which he has pressed for action with regard to the needs of agriculture in his area.
If this government would raise the standard of eastern agriculture, for which it must assume responsibility, and follow courses similar to those which raised the standards in western Canada, a great change might be accomplished. When we came to office, as far as western Canada was concerned it was 20220-333
Federal-Provincial Relations just another of those forgotten areas and the reason was simply this; that the Liberal party had reached the conclusion that the west would vote Liberal no matter how they were treated here. Hon. members opposite have the same view about some other parts of Canada today. One of the things needed to strengthen confederation and bring about new confidence is action under ARDA and in other areas of agriculture to which reference will be made by other speakers in this debate. I am convinced of that. Constitutional matters dominate the thinking of some people; whereas the people as a whole are affected by economic conditions. Certainly agriculture, not only in Quebec and Ontario but also in the maritimes, needs a new approach and far more consideration than it has been receiving during the last 15 months.
What is the substance of the resolution introduced by the minister? I am afraid that it is simply more tinkering with the problem. The divisions of confederation, or the cracks in the structure-I do not believe they are great, but they are becoming more significant
cannot be repaired by papering them over. That is what is being done here. In other words the action perhaps effective for the moment in so far as the provinces are concerned, will not solve the major problem of confederation.
When we were in office we had a number of conferences. I will deal with them when we come to second reading. I have already pointed out that our plan was to strengthen confederation, to open our northern areas and resource areas outside the ordinary ambit of provincial opportunity or ability to develop. We made available $7i million to each and every province for this purpose. We brought in programs of which I have already spoken; winter works, vocational training in order to strengthen and extend opportunities for individuals. We met the immediate problem by a tremendous increase
in amounts available to the provinces_________
amounts that when read into the record must be regarded as eye-opening.
I am not going to review at this time in particular what we did, but I want to generalize to this extent. When we came into office the provincial governments received 10 per cent of the income tax, 9 per cent of corporation tax and 50 per cent of succession duties. We immediately raised the 9 per cent to 13 per cent. On January 1, I960, we made available 1 per cent of the corporation tax to the province of Quebec in lieu

Federal-Provincial Relations of university grants. In addition, on January 1, 1962, we increased the 13 per cent to 16 per cent for income tax, with an accelerating 1 per cent for every year.
When the present government came into office, with the agreements we had put into effect in 1963 the share of the provincial governments was 17 per cent; in 1964 it is 18 per cent. We made available hundreds of millions of dollars to the provinces which otherwise they would not have received. I am not going to say that we ever received regard or appreciation for this. The Minister of Finance will find out, that having been done, it will not be remembered. These are things that are forgotten. I am sure the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, with his many years of experience as premier of one of our provinces, will agree with me that you never get any thanks for what you did. It is as old as the days of Senator Clay. I am sure the Minister of Finance has read very thoroughly the history of that period from 1830 to 1850 in the United States, and those great debates of Webster, Clay and Calhoun. Clay once went to somebody and said, "I hope you are supporting me this time". This was back in 1832. He said, "I have fixed up your uncle with a post office, and I have made provision for your father with a pension". He was referring to a pension arising out of the war of 1812. The reply was, "Oh, yes; you did all this, Senator Clay. But what are you going to do now?" The question was, not what he had done but what he would do. The minister will find that out when he has had as much experience in public life as he had in private business.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext: There isn't enough time left for me.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
And, I hope, with great success in public life. These things will be accepted and within hours, or days, or months, human nature being what it is, the provinces will say, "But what are you going to do next? This is all very fine; we have these things now-but what are you going to do?" That brings me to the larger field as to what courses should be taken now. I have already pointed out that during our period of office we brought the provinces to a new plateau of fiscal capability to enable them the better to deal with their constitutional responsibilities. With the additional hundreds of millions of dollars we provided, they were able to embark on new and far reaching programs in education, highways and resource management.

We did something more. We did away with the tax rental plan. So long as the tax rental plan was in effect, the provinces were in a subservient and subordinate position. In other words, we reversed the 20 years' centralization trend toward a unitary state in Canada. We freed the provinces from the strait-jacket to which they had been confined by years of centralization. We raised the revenues of all provinces to new heights. We brought into effect an evolutionary process, new programs and policies under joint responsibility heretofore incapable of being financed. Our purpose, our aim, our determination was to return to the principles and spirit of the British North America Act; to strengthen the fabric of confederation-above all, to assure that in co-operation with the provinces we would guarantee all Canadians, regardless of their postal address or regional economic differences, reasonable economic equality.
Dealing with this question in the house on September 27, 1961, I said:
We are going to restore as far as it is possible the inherent principles of the constitution.
I had been pointing out that they had been departed from.
The then Minister of Transport as he is now, was in the house. Certainly when the King administration started to move in the direction of centralization, followed by the St. Laurent administration, no one ever expected that those pathways of experiment in wartime would become the highways of peace. But they did.
I was interrupted by the present Minister of Transport in these words:
There were no deficits in our day.
No, there were not. There was no reason for deficits because the provinces were being starved. We increased social security payments by approximately 46 per cent during our period of office. We made vast developments in agriculture and industry. But I repeat if it had not been for our concern for confederation, there would have been no deficits.
Speaking on that occasion, September 27, 1961, I said that we had restored the inherent principles of the constitution, which was something we undertook to do. I said that we were ending centralization and putting in its place co-operation within the principles of the constitution. Hon. gentlemen opposite talk today about co-operative federalism. All I can say is that the translation of co-operative federalism into action has denied every basic principle of confederation, Co-operatior

can only come through consultation; and in too many cases this government has consulted after making a decision to take a certain course regardless of the attitude of the provinces.
We determined to bring to Canada the capacity to amend our own constitution. So many people say today that the constitution has to be amended in regard to certain matters and this after 97 years of experience. But in those important portions of the constitution as embodied in the British North America Act, sections 91 and 92, changes cannot take place without the unanimous consent of each and every province. It is so easy to talk about it; but let us remember, Mr. Chairman, that rights of religion and education are inviolable and unchangeable. The division of responsibilities between the federal parliament and provincial legislatures cannot be changed by the simple exigencies of the government of Canada or by the action of one or more provinces.
I read so frequently of great speeches made outside the House of Commons about what is going to be done to bring about a new constitution. It is, if I may use a colloquialism, eyewash to say that the constitution which we have we Will hold, but that the changes which we want will be made on the basis of the desires of one, two or three provinces. That cannot be done. These changes can only come into effect by general and unanimous agreement.
I realize, as did the minister in his statement the other day, how complex this matter is and how difficult is the problem of dominion-provincial relations. It was easy when in opposition for those who now sit opposite to make those statements. But they have found that it is difficult to pound out on the anvil of experience the theories so airily announced during the election campaigns.
Today I am looking at the whole picture of the kind of Canada which I see; not a picture of a series of sovereign states, but of one Canada maintaining the constitutional rights which are the essence of confederation; the equal partnership of those of English and French origin who brought about confederation within our country.
I do not see in that respect, a Canada far removed from the Canada of Cartier and Macdonald. Read the debates, Mr. Chairman, of 1864, 1865 and 1866. Those men faced a tremendous challenge and they met it in cooperation. They did not dream of a Canada bifurcated or multiplicated-if that word can be used-divided and uncertain. They envisaged a central government which could 20220-333i
Federal-Provincial Relations discharge its responsibilities. They thought of provincial legislatures which would be able to maintain within their limits and territorial boundaries the things dear to those areas and provinces.
Those who say that simply by wishing you can erase the past have not absorbed history. It is easy to say those things. In my boyhood in western Canada the farmers used to talk of separating western Canada from the rest. They said: "We should be removed. Our markets are north and south. We pay a tremendous price for the tariff policy of the country as a whole". Those voices were stilled by the calmness of the leaders of that time. I recall very well an occasion in 1957 when I spoke in one of the maritime provinces at a large meeting. I was dealing with conditions existing at the time and I received a very friendly reception. But I was followed by a former premier of Prince Edward Island, Dr. MacMillan. He thanked me, but his thanks extended into maritime rights, and by the time he was through that audience was ready to fight, so aroused they were by the injustices of confederation. Leaders in the maritimes have taken strong stands, but they have always come back to one thing, that we stand together as one nation, one Canada. If we start breaking up the country into segments we destroy not only the hopes of the fathers of confederation, but our hope that we will be able to hand on to those that follow a Canada worthy of the heritage which is ours.
What are some of the things that can be done in this connection? The time has come to convene a conference of representatives of the federal and provincial governments of this nation representing the various parties in all of the provinces, to examine the whole field of Canadian confederation-not a conference lasting two days, but a conference in which, in a spirit of Canadian co-operation and pride, they will meet together and endeavour through discussion and consultation to arrive at decisions regarding the future of this nation. Can it be done? If it cannot be done, then the hopes of amendments of an important nature to our constitution have ceased to exist.
Sir John A. Macdonald, who having regard to the contribution he made to confederation has not been remembered as he should be as the father of his country, a designation given him by no less a great Canadian leader than Sir Wilfrid Laurier, said during the last years of his life:
I have no accord with the desire expressed in some quarters that by any mode whatever there

Federal-Provincial Relations should be an attempt made to oppress one language or to render it inferior to the other. I believe it would be impossible if it were tried and it would be foolish and wicked if it were possible.
That has been the stand of Conservative leaders through succeeding generations, and Liberal leaders too. The agreements relating to this partnership, found in section 133 of the British North America Act, and sections 91 and 92, to which I have already referred, jurisdiction over education, are the very bedrock of confederation.
Such a conference will be able to do what no royal commission can do. A royal commission can sit, hear and ultimately recommend but finally the matter must come to the representatives of the federal parliament and the provincial legislatures.
We sought to repatriate the constitution when we were in office. We had a number of conferences and we had almost achieved success when two provinces had reservations with regard to certain sections, and we did not achieve repatriation. The issue was not the basis of amendments to the constitution but simply to bring the constitution to Canada.
I hear people talking about the symbols of a nation. How many of them realize that we are the only country in the British family of nations or the commonwealth of today that cannot amend its own constitution? We tried to do so. We went a long way in that direction in a desire to conciliate without loss of principle, but without success in achieving repatriation. Such a conference could suggest ways and means of repatriating the constitution. It could also make recommendations as to a national flag and the other symbols of national sovereignty. There would be representatives there of all the political parties and they would not meet in the glare of publicity. As the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam knows, whenever we were behind closed doors in dominion-provincial conferences we made a great deal more progress than when we were under the glare of publicity. That is human nature. We went to work there. Let this conference meet in that way. Can you tell me any other way in which success can be achieved?
I have studied this question. There is no portion of the constitutional debates since 1762 that I have not read. What has Canada achieved? The Minister of Justice knows. It was the first country within what is the commonwealth of today to have freedom of religion, not by our own action but by the action of the British parliament. It was the first one to abolish slavery, the first one to
IMr. Diefenbaker.]
give a Jewish person the opportunity to serve as a result of legislation passed in Lower Canada. Canada was the first country in what is now the commonwealth to bring about responsible government which made possible the commonwealth of today. The Lafontaines and the Baldwins, these men saw Canada as a great nation, one nation. Cartier said it over and over again. He said, "I can accept no other proposition", while demanding, as did Laurier many times, that there should be full partnership.
Sir, this conference would examine the whole position of biculturalism and bilingualism. I have endeavoured to think of what other course could be taken that would bring Canadians together. I do not know what it is. I do not want to see us separated and divided. Why can we not, in the spirit of the fathers of confederation, meet in such a conference?
I recall the 26th of February, 1963, when I received the honour of the freedom of the city of London in that historic place, the Guildhall, an honour that I deeply appreciated. Only a few days before I went over there I found for the first time that the Constitutional Act, which was an amendment of the Quebec Act, was introduced on that very day in 1792. There was history, there was tradition, there was something of the pride of achievement. To my left was the great monument of William Pitt, the younger. On that day, the 26th of February, 1792, in the parliament of the United Kingdom a debate took place regarding French-English relations in the Canada of that time. Read that debate. It is the most thrilling debate you can read. William Pitt, the younger, Charles James Fox, Edmund Burke and Sheridan, too, said, we are going to build in North America a country where two races will live side by side in amity and co-operation. It is very interesting when one looks back in this way. You recall other things. You recall the famous quarrel between Burke and Fox which took place on that occasion. They were great friends, but they never spoke again. It was all over the question of whether the legislative council of Upper and Lower Canada should be hereditary, as a peerage. Two of them said, let us have a peerage in Canada; let us not just appoint members of the legislative council for life; let us have a peerage. I think it was Fox who said if we had had a peerage in the 13 colonies in 1776, those 13 colonies would still be with us. Burke took the opposite stand. They separated. Read that debate;

it is one of the most thrilling expositions of the relationships between races.
Sir, the whole field of federal-provincial relations should be looked into on a long term basis. The provinces must be placed in a position where they can fully discharge their responsibilities. If you simply hand a little more from time to time to the provinces, all you are doing is postponing the day when more is requested. Human nature is the same for groups as for individuals. If we get so much today, then we say we will try to get a little more tomorrow, so on you go with the problem and it is never solved. As more and more revenues are passed to the provinces-unless responsibilities are being passed on-the more serious becomes the situation for the federal authority. This is the reason why many believe there should be a constitutional realignment of responsibilities.
Now, that is one field. I should like to refer to another field which arises directly out of provincial jurisdiction, and that is the field of urban improvement. The municipalities are the creatures of the provincial legislatures and are responsible to them for their existence and fiscal powers. With the extent to which more and more Canadians are moving into the great cities, with the vast changes, the splurge as it were in the suburban areas, is it not appropriate that such a conference should give consideration, in co-operation, to providing for a national policy for urban development and renewal? A co-ordinated policy is beyond the means of the urban areas and, beyond the means of the provinces. Urban renewal is a national problem today. It is a national problem, just as it was in the days when the forebears of the Minister of Trade and Commerce went into western Canada. The opening of western Canada was a national problem. It has changed now. Today they find themselves in a position where the days of the pioneer are past. Today, in so far as the urban areas of our country are concerned, we as a nation need to do some constitutional pioneering. It will require agreement, it will require consultation between federal and provincial authorities. However it is something that will have to be met. This sprawling urban and suburban complex that has developed in all parts of our country, as in the United States, is one of the greatest problems we face.
There are many members here who have had municipal experience. They know how tremendous is the challenge of this problem.
Federal-Provincial Relations This is another matter to which consideration should be given by such a conference. I say to the Minister of Finance-I know he has that diffidence that a minister of finance must possess in not allowing any of us to anticipate any fiscal changes in advance-that one of the first steps that should be taken in our country in that connection, aside from this conference, is that young couples should be encouraged to own their own homes and that effective consideration must be given to allowing deductible items from taxable income. I am referring in particular to municipal taxes on homes. These are things that will benefit national development in our cities.
There should be set up a department of urban affairs to co-ordinate the various activities of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and other agencies dealing with urban aspects, such as housing, sewage loans and the financing of industrial development. It has been done in the United Kingdom. There of course there is a unitary state. We must here act in co-operation and consultation. What about urban decay, responsible in a large measure for juvenile delinquency, parks and recreation areas, the social improvements that are necessary for this nation, rapid transit systems to relieve traffic congestion, the throughways that are essential to the conduct of commercial affairs? I could go on. After all, we are approaching the centennial of confederation, and this is a massive problem. This is one that will require a concerted approach on a nation-wide scale with federal-provincial co-operation following full consultation.
Finally, sir, I return to agriculture in eastern Canada. If we are to meet the demands, the proper demands of the people, many of the criticisms and attitudes which would lead to separatism will be avoided by action in assuring that farmers in eastern Canada, the maritimes and elsewhere shall have a reasonable share of the national income.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this legislation to amend the federal-provincial tax sharing arrangements is extremely important. It is important because fiscal matters are at the root of much of the federal-provincial bickering and rancour that has taken place from time to time ever since confederation.
Sometimes it is suggested that federal and provincial governments do not get along because they happen to be of different political parties and because there are personalities involved, but if one examines the record he finds this is not true, that irrespective of

Federal-Provincial Relations the political party in office at a particular time, in a province or in Ottawa, these differences continue to exist because they are based on the need for money on the part of the provinces.
I think it was Chick Sales who once said that when a fellow says it isn't the money, it's the principle of the thing-it's the money. That has been true with federal-provincial relations. Many of the difficulties that are put forth are really superficial, and the basic differences are fiscal. The fact is that the provinces are faced with growing responsibilities. The responsibilities given to them under the British North America Act have grown in geometric progression throughout the years and the revenues available to the provinces to discharge those responsibilities have not grown proportionately.
We have come to the time in confederation when the federal government must either assume some of those responsibilities or it must make a larger share of the tax revenues available to the provinces so that they can do the job which has constitutionally been allocated to them. I want to point out that even with all the additional revenue which the federal government has made available to the provinces, that even with the legislation which is now before us put into effect, the provinces will still get only about 30 per cent of the revenue from the shared tax fields and the federal government will get 70 per cent. This still leaves the provinces with a relatively small share of this vast tax revenue that is available to finance government services in Canada.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that this is Canada's No. 1 problem. The right hon. Leader of the Opposition has made a useful suggestion in putting forth the idea of a federal-provincial conference, one which would be held for a considerable period of time and on which there would be a great deal of preliminary work, so that we can work out some division of fields of tax revenue or reallocation of responsibilities, so that we do not have this constant haggling between the federal and provincial governments.
If we neglect this matter the strain and the stress on confederation will continue and could eventually destroy confederation. If I may paraphrase Santayana, he said something like this, that those who are unwilling to learn the lessons of history are condemned to repeat its mistakes. Unless we in this parliament are prepared to see the trend in federal-provincial relations and try to grapple with the problem head on, then I am convinced that some very difficult days lie ahead for confederation.

I have a very limited time, Mr. Chairman, and therefore I am going to apply myself only to the proposed amendments arising out of the two federal-provincial conferences, the one held in November 1963 and the one held in April of this year. Let me deal first with the proposals arising out of the November conference. They can be divided mainly into three parts.
First of all, the federal government is prepared to equalize the revenue from the standard tax rates up to the average of the two top provinces. I hasten at once to say that this is an improvement over what we have had before, when the equalization formula only brought the provinces up to the national average. Certainly the average of the top two is better than the national average, but I cannot forbear pointing out that this is not what the Liberal party promised just about 15 months ago. What it promised was that it would equalize up to the highest province in Canada.
I could give many quotations. Already the Leader of the Opposition has quoted from the book, "The Liberal Party", by the Minister of Transport, in which he said:
At the national Liberal convention of 1958, the party pledged itself to alter the basis of equalization payments so that the revenues of all provinces from income taxes and succession duties would be brought up to the level of the province having the highest per capita revenue.
I point out that the booklet called, "The Liberals Have the Answer"-they may have the answer but it is a little slow in coming through-stated:
The Liberal party.. .believes that, in order to ensure a basic equality of provincial services between all parts of Canada, all provinces should receive an equal revenue per head of population from the tax fields shared between the two levels of government so that all Canadian citizens will benefit equally.
I remind the committee that the Prime Minister himself, opening the conference last November, said in his statement, at page 14:
It is well known that my colleagues and I prefer to see equalization paid up to the level, not of the average of all the provinces as parliament enacted in 1961, but up to the level of the highest.
That is quite specific.
Why would the government equalize to the two top provinces? I say quite categorically that this was a matter of cooking a formula to get the kind of results it wanted rather than adopting the formula to which it had committed itself, a formula that would have treated all the provinces equally and justly.
The second change which this legislation is proposing is that from now on part of the

revenue from natural resources will be taken into account in computing equalization payments. It is to be based on one half of the amount by which natural resource revenue on a per capita basis exceeds the national average. Again this is not in keeping with the commitments made by the Liberal party when it was seeking office.
I can refer to many quotations but I just refer to the Prime Minister's own statement in this house on June 2, 1958, as recorded at page 733 of Hansard for the date:
Not only Is the principle important, but the application of that principle is even more important. On what basis are equalization payments going to be made?
As far as this party is concerned we are pledged to equalization on the basis of the per capita yield of the three taxes in the wealthiest province.
There is nothing there about taking into consideration natural resources revenue. I wish to ask the government, why is this particular source of revenue taken into account when computing equalization payments. Why is this chosen as a criterion? There is no suggestion that gasoline tax revenue or revenue from automobile licences or sales tax or liquor revenues should be included. Why select this one field? Again, this was the best way to cook the books in order to get the result the government wanted. What they are doing thereby is to penalize those provinces which are making the maximum use of their resources and seeking to get the maximum revenue from them.
Resource revenue, I would point out, does not represent clear gain. The provinces which derive revenue from their resources have to spend large sums of money on the development and conservation of those resources. If this is to be taken into consideration, then the revenue considered ought to be net revenue, if it is considered at all.
In addition, as one hon. member has just pointed out, what is involved is the sale of a capital asset-the sale of something which is not necessarily recurring. Moreover, the present formula bestows a great benefit on those provinces which have already sold their capital assets and disposed of their resources. The provinces adversely affected by this legislation are provinces such as Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia. The older provinces which have disposed of their assets in many cases, are those who will benefit. Just make a comparison. The revenue on a per capita basis from natural resources in Ontario is $6.91. In Saskatchewan it is $22.57 and in British Columbia it is $33.72. Does any person in his right mind contend
Federal-Provincial Relations that in the province of Ontario with its vast mining complex and its great timber industry, $6.91 per capita represents the economic value of the natural resources? Of course it does not. Putting natural resource revenue into the formula for computing equalization payments is discriminating against the more recently developed provinces and is working hardship upon them.
The interesting thing is this. When we come to the third amendment, the government turns a complete somersault. The third proposal is that the abatement for succession duties will be raised from 50 per cent to 75 per cent. That is fine, I agree with that. But the government says that this increased abatement will not be considered for equalization purposes. The first 50 per cent is to be taken into account for equalization purposes, but not the additional 25 per cent. Will the minister tell this committee why natural resource revenue will be taken into consideration in computing equalization payments but succession duty revenue will not be taken into consideration. As a matter of fact there is more reason to take into account succession duty revenue which, although it is paid in a province, is levied in many cases on wealth which has been earned all over Canada, whereas revenue which comes from natural resources comes as a result of the investment and the efforts of the province itself. If the federal government wants to include natural resources in computing equalization payments they should certainly have included the increased succession duty abatement.
In my opinion if ever there was a case of cooking a formula so as to get a specific result, this is it. Instead of starting out, as their own program dictated, to work out a formula which would be fair to all the provinces on some reasonable basis, the federal government, far from equalizing to the highest province, has equalized to the two top provinces, then goes on to bring in an entirely extraneous factor-the revenue from resource development-and then, to make doubly sure that they get the result they want, say the additional 25 per cent abatement on succession duty will not be taken into consideration when computing equalization. I have attended a good many federal-provincial conferences and I have seen some of the fiscal experts set up a goal and then work out a formula which would get them what they sought. But I have never seen it done so clumsily and so blatantly as in this case. This represents in my opinion sheer discrimination.
I see it is five o'clock.
