The house resumed from Thursday, July 2, consideration of the motion (Mr. Orlikow):
That an order of the house do issue for a copy of all government statements and directives to government departments during the past year regarding security procedures and investigations.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. S. Macdonald (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
At the conclusion of the debate last week I made some reference to the defence of Canada regulations and particularly to the suggestion made by certain hon. members opposite that the procedure which should be followed in these security matters should resemble the procedure outlined in those regulations.
I thought it would be useful to investigate that suggestion further and having done so, and particularly having talked to one of the gentlemen responsible for enforcing these regulations, I find that contrary to what has been suggested time again in this house the procedure followed under those regulations was not a judicial procedure. It was essentially the same as the Prime Minister put forward in his speech of October 25. It was a procedure set up entirely within the administration. Hon.

members can confirm this themselves by examining the regulations. The advisory committees set up in those circumstances were set up solely for the purpose of advising the minister with respect to internment proceedings. They were not a court of record. There was no right of appeal. The proceedings were not within reach of the prerogative writs. In particular, there was no right to confront crown witnesses, and only such evidence was made available as the committee in its discretion thought desirable.
In particular I would like to emphasize that there was no right, as I think has been suggested from time to time, on behalf of people who might be affected by that type of order, to confront witnesses or examine evidence presented on behalf of the crown. Quite the contrary: the only right individuals had in that particular case was to learn of the allegations made against them on behalf of the crown in the most general terms.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North last week took exception to my suggestion that he had proposed the confrontation of witnesses in this proceeding. I find, on examining the record, that I was mistaken and his intervention was quite correct. Rather, the suggestion that witnesses should be confronted, that it should be possible for a person affected by this tribunal to examine those witnesses in a proceeding resembling a court of law, was made by his leader, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) and more particularly in a speech he made in this house on June 3, 1963, which may be found at page 593 of Hansard for that date.
I would point out, as has been pointed out before with regard to this type of case, that in view of the counter-espionage type of structure, the security structure, which is involved, it would be most deleterious and would have a very serious effect on the security measures which are taken on behalf of all the people of Canada to submit the investigations and reports of the security officials to a legal type cross-examination.
I think it would be most useful to reemphasize to the house, in connection with this question, the basic function of the security screening in this particular type of case. I would remind the house, first, that the interests of Canadians generally require that certain state secrets be shielded from unfriendly eyes. Unhappily we had an incident in recent months which came very close to this chamber, indicating that representatives of foreign powers continue to

engage in operations to obtain access to Canadian state secrets. Second, Mr. Speaker, I would point out that the best and surest shield for our state secrets is by entrusting them to servants of unimpeachable loyalty, servants who are free from any pressures either of family, personal background or ideology which could possibly result from time to time in a conflict with such loyalty. Particularly I would point out and would ask the house to bear in mind that the determination of this question as to the loyalty or non-loyalty, the reliability or non-reliability of any particular servant is a very difficult matter. This is not only so from the very essence of the subject matter, but also from the fact that those who with unfriendly design are seeking access to our secrets will take elaborate precautions to conceal their intent; and even more so, those people who may have personal weaknesses but are otherwise loyal-weaknesses which make them particularly subject to exploitation by the unscrupulous-will take very careful precautions to conceal those weaknesses. We must bear in mind that secrets are one species of state property of a particularly sensitive nature. By their very nature, their exposure to the public spoils them. They are not like the stone of Scone or the crown jewels which, if stolen, can be recovered and restored undamaged. Once they are made available to the public, once they are made available to unfriendly eyes, their very distinctive characteristic of property is lost. They are at once so precious and so sensitive a form of state property that we have had to adopt, and in fact all civilized democratic countries have had to adopt, very special measures in respect of their defence.
In particular, in respect of measures required to protect security we have had to abandon, at least in part, some of the concepts of fair procedure and open trial which we normally use in our legal proceedings. One of the great experts on jurisprudence has pointed out that the three watchwords of justice and the rule of law in a democratic state are openness, fairness and impartiality. As I have mentioned, by the very nature of the material, openness or exposure to publicity is one thing that is not possible in security questions. I have also pointed out that impartiality in this case is somewhat difficult, because who can be impartial with the security of the country at stake? It is obviously necessary for an onus to lie in favour of the crown with regard to those who would have access to its secrets. But I do think we 20220-334
Motions for Papers
can continue to require the observation of principles of fairness in connection with these security provisions, and I think these principles of fairness can aptly be given effect to and carried out under the procedure proposed by the Prime Minister on October 25.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to set out in point form the procedure which will be followed and which has been followed in connection with these security procedures since the Prime Minister's announcement last fall. First, where an employee is in the situation that his reliability has been put in doubt, he has the right to be told that his reliability is subject to doubt and he has the right to learn, so far as it is possible from a security standpoint, the reasons for such doubt. Second, he will have the opportunity to give his side of the particular case, to frame his own case, in respect of the allegations which are made against him. Third, he will be entitled to a second hearing by the head of the agency which is responsbile for his work, and if the decision remains unfavourable, the case will be submitted to a board of review made up of senior civil servants who have not been previously directly involved in the particular case.
The protection of state security is, as I have said, a matter of critical importance. One cannot assure people who may be adversely affected by security screening procedures that they will work in every instance, because after all, being of human creation these procedures are necessarily fallible. It is my submission to the house that the measures proposed by this government to the house do apply a high degree of fairness. It is for this reason, and because of the confidential nature of the document involved, that I would request the hon. member for Winnipeg North, or his colleagues on his behalf, to withdraw his request for the exposure of this particular document.

Mr. Speaker, could I ask the hon. member a question before he sits down? Could he elaborate a little more this appeal to the board made up of senior civil servants? Does the person whose reliability is in doubt have the opportunity to appear personally, with counsel; or do they merely review the written documents having to do with the case?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This has been more eloquently stated by the Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker; but I would point out to the hon. member that he will have the right to appear before this particular board and put his best case forward. It is also my understanding

Motions for Papers
that he will have the benefit of counsel in defending himself in what is essentially not a legal proceeding but one in which considerations of a legal character may arise.
The hon. member said "he will have". Do I assume that he has now, under this directive?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member can take it that I am speaking not only of the future, but of the present and what dates back to October 25, in what I have said.

Mr. Speaker, I do not suppose anybody in this house could disagree with the general observations of the parliamentary secretary who has just spoken with regard to the importance of security or, indeed, the desirability of the safeguards for the individual which he says are incorporated in the procedure. But it is my respectful submission to the house that these observations entirely miss the point that is before the house in this motion, which is whether or not the government will disclose to the members of the house the form of procedure which has been decided upon by the government as the security procedure which is to affect those many thousands of people whose whole livelihood and security may be at stake in this important matter.
I urge upon all members of the house, although not too many of them are here at the moment, the acceptance of this particular motion, because I suggest a basic principle is involved which has been overlooked in what we have heard to date. I would put this basic principle in this way: Is the right of parliament to scrutinize the nature of the security procedures affecting the employment and the firing of thousands of government employees to be defeated by hocus-pocus or gobbledygook about the need to keep secret even the procedure by which an aggrieved employee can vindicate his right to his livelihood, and to his reputation, upon which his livelihood depends?
Let me remind the house of the background to this matter. Last year after a number of very disturbing incidents resulting in the dismissal of some persons from the services and other persons employed in the public service on security grounds-which grounds turned out to be completely unfounded-the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) gave an assurance that new security procedures were being devised which would give an employee or a prospective employee the opportunity of resolving any doubt as to his or her being

a security risk, and second, would enable a second look to be taken by what might be described as an internal tribunal. The minister of justice of that day, Hon. Lionel Chevrier, assured the house that the "new and carefully devised procedures will improve our measures and give new assurance to individual employees". Note, Mr. Speaker, the words "assurance to individual employees".
In the debate last Thursday two facts emerged. First of all, it was stated that the proposed new procedures have been incorporated in a single directive; so that we have an existing document which incorporates these so-called new procedures, which give an assurance to the employees concerned and also to the members of this house. Second, that the terms of this document-and this is on the record in a formal answer given to the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orli-kow)-have been communicated to all government departments.
The return given went on to say that the government does not regard it as customary to inform employees or their associations of its terms, or to table a document of this type in the house. In other words, Mr. Speaker, after giving an assurance to parliament that the government will take steps to correct inadequate security procedures, it then refuses to give to the house the steps which it has taken. It proffers assurances to employees and then refuses to tell the employees what are the assurances.
What is the good, Mr. Speaker, of telling us that there are adequate procedures if we are not to see them written down in black and white, and if the house is to be denied knowledge of them? I go so far as to say that this is a ridiculous situation and a serious affront to parliament. Are we not to be entrusted even with a statement on the principles upon which those affected in these so-called security cases are to have their rights determined, to whom they are to apply, and what the nature of the procedure, or the appeal if it be an appeal, may happen to be? If that is the case I suggest, as I said before, that it is an affront to parliament.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) asks us to draw a veil of secrecy over the whole matter. Like some high priest of the modern age he mumbles the word "security" and we are then supposed to be satisfied. There is no one in the house, Mr. Speaker, who is asking that the means by which this security information is gathered be publicly revealed. However, there are some things I should like

to know. For instance, I would be interested in knowing the type of questionnaire used to pry into the private lives of would-be employees of the government. I would be interested in knowing whether electronic or so-called "bugging" devices or wire tapping is used in this regard. In the United States a special government information subcommittee of the committee on government operations is inquiring into this very matter of which I have been speaking, to determine whether the right means are used. But is this parliament to be more security conscious even than the congress of the United States of America? My point, Mr. Speaker, once more, is that we are not inquiring as to the means by which information is secured.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question at this point, because it may be somewhat germane to his case. The Minister of Justice indicated in his statement last week that the particular document which this motion asks for contains material which, in itself, would be prejudicial to this particular means of gaining information. The hon. member is saying, on the one hand, that he does not want to expose this means, but on the other hand he is insisting on having the document. Does he not think that that is a reasonable explanation for its non-disclosure? I would ask him that question, Mr. Speaker.

Surely, Mr. Speaker, in setting out the rights of employees to a hearing, the type of hearing they may have and the type of particulars to be given, this sort of document is the sort which I assume the Prime Minister was talking about when he gave assurances to the house that this new procedure would be developed and would be embodied in some form of directive, if not regulation. We are told that there is a directive. I do not know whether incorporated in this directive for some reason unknown to me is some mysterious disclosure as to the source of the information which should not be made available. That may be so. If it is so, a very simple solution suggests itself, and that is that a proper directive be prepared and made available to the members of this house. If the Minister of Justice or the parliamentary secretary had said: "In our directive incorporated in certain procedural rules which deal with these matters there is unfortunately highly confidential information which should be made known only to heads of government departments", that is one thing. But no; we are told that the whole 20220-334*
Motions for Papers
procedure has been set out in a single directive, that it is available to all government departments, but is to be denied to parliament. The information cannot be so terribly confidential or secret, or surely it would not be made available as a departmental document to various persons in the departments.
If the parliamentary secretary can say that there is or there will be a suitable document prepared setting out the rules which affect those who are dismissed, or those who seek employment but are denied it on security grounds, and such promise were made, I am sure the hon. member for Winnipeg North would be happy to hear it and I think this motion might well be withdrawn. But no such suggestion has been made and we are pressing this matter.
I said that we are not seeking the source of the security information, nor are we asking for the disclosure of the evidence upon which decisions are made. All we are asking is that the written rules of procedure enacted for the protection of employees or those who would be employees be disclosed to the house and to those whom they affect. How do we know otherwise that the rules are adequate or fair, or that they take account of the rights of individuals? How can we as individual members of parliament advise those who are concerned with these matters? I have always been under the impression that one of the basic duties of a member of parliament, indeed of parliament itself, was to protect the rights of individuals against injustice. How can we carry out this vital task if we are not to know even the procedural rules under which bureaucracy is working its will in regard to these people?
The government calls itself a Liberal government. Perhaps I have had a misunderstanding of the meaning of the word "liberal". I thought the word "liberal" connoted a concern with the rights of the individual, but perhaps we will be told, as in the cases of immigrants, that they have no rights. Immigrants are daily subjected to farcical hearings where they are not informed of the objections to their entry, and we are told they are without rights. I wonder whether that argument will be applied here. Is it to be said of the 205,000 civil servants, the 121,000 or more people employed in government corporations, the 123,000 or more people in the armed services, that once the word "security" is mentioned their livelihood, their reputations, can be blasted and they are not told anything about it or even the procedure by which they can have the allegation checked?

Motions for Papers
In my view there is nothing more serious than that a person's reputation and his livelihood can be dealt with by these secret procedures, of which we are not to know the details. I would have thought that a Liberal government worthy of the name would disregard the sort of timorous hocus-pocus we hear from time to time that tells us that parliament itself is to be denied information as to procedures which affect the livelihood and reputation of a tremendously large group of civil servants and other Canadians.
In the United States, which is not known for being unduly tender to people when security is concerned, they have a directive in this regard. The number of it escapes me at the moment although I have it somewhere. It is a specific directive dealing with this matter. Does anybody think that in the British House of Commons the government can get away with saying: We have devised some security procedures but we are not going to tell you what they are; we are not going to put them in writing for you. We will make some general statements and you must satisfy yourselves with that. I do not believe a government would last very long in that country if it adopted that sort of attitude.
I appeal to the government to change its mind. They will have time to do so because I imagine that this debate will not conclude today. I sincerely hope that if the government does not change its mind and make available to the house at least in outline form the security procedures which it says it has devised, including the new ones which it says fill the gaps that existed before, parliament will show enough self-respect to compel the government to do so.

Mr. Speaker, I will not have too much to say. I had thought I would be in another room. I was about to say "in another place" but probably those are not the right words to use today. So the pearls of wisdom which I propose to cast before the members of the government will not be as lengthy as they would have been otherwise, or as the government feared they might have been.
After listening to the tail end of the argument made by the parliamentary secretary and after reading what took place in the debate on July 2, I am reminded that the government's attitude in this matter is reminiscent of a Roman emperor, not the one who fiddled, although that allusion might well apply too in some respects, but the Roman emperor who, being compelled by custom and by law to make his laws public, saw

that they were printed upon stone tablets but then had the tablets set up so high that nobody could read them. I think that pretty well exemplifies the attitude of the government in this connection.
If I may go back to the initiation of this debate by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), as found on page 4954 of Hansard he quotes what the Prime Minister said on October 25 when this matter was first discussed. I am not going to quarrel so much with the refusal of the government to disclose all of the facts which are related in the first paragraph of the quotation, although some fault can be found with their failure to disclose at least a part of them. However, the second paragraph deals with the rules of what is in effect, I submit, an appeal and I take exception to what is set out there.
True enough, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) indicated that this was an administrative matter. Certainly so far as security directives are concerned the government has a very grave responsibility and I would be the first one to deny that they must be compelled to produce all of the directives they issue with regard to the question of security. But once it becomes apparent that an individual employee may be subject to dismissal in so far as his status and job are concerned, a very important aspect of his life, and the matter then becomes the subject of scrutiny by a board, my submission is that even though the board may be an administrative board this is in effect a quasi-judicial proceeding. The administrative aspect is dissolved into a judicial consideration. This is a review, an appeal, and when there is a discretion to be exercised it must and should be exercised in a judicial way.
This has been said over and over again not only in the courts but by political philosophers. A discretionary right exercised by a review board with respect to any matter affecting the government should be exercised in a judicial way. How can it be exercised in a judicial way if the person who is the subject of the inquiry is not made aware of the procedures which will be adopted, the basis of the charge against him and provided with an adequate opportunity to meet that charge and to present his side of the story? With great deference to the views expressed by the Minister of Justice and his parliamentary secretary, I submit with respect to at least the second part of the proposed new procedures outlined by the Prime Minister

that the government has no real justification in refusing to disclose the detail of these directives.
Having said that, I would point out that there are ways by which this house could be put in a position to consider the matter. It is a very important matter and it might well be that it could be submitted to a committee in camera. The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) said this might involve hundreds, possibly thousands of people before this procedure faded into something completely different. Why not let the matter be discussed in a committee in camera so the government might have the benefit of the views and suggestions of hon. members in this house who, having been invested with the confidence of the people of this country, should have an opportunity in this way of communicating their suggestions to the government.
I am sure that the members of the government would be the last ones to suggest that they had reached perfection in a matter of this kind. This is a very small, timorous step in a direction in which they should have taken brave and bold action many years before. Having in mind the fact that there will be advances, I think, there will be changes and improvements, I would think it would be the part of wisdom for a government to discuss the matter perhaps in a standing committee or a special committee established for the purpose at an in camera sitting.
I suggest that, as a first step, the government might give serious consideration to placing before such a committee all the relevant facts and documentary evidence in regard to what has been done to implement what the Prime Minister indicated would be done by way of establishing appeal procedure. I do not need to stop there. I think the hon. member for Greenwood dealt with this as well. I quite appreciate the fact that the government would be in violation of its duty if it did disclose certain aspects of its directives. Surely however it is competent for them to examine, with great care, everything which is comprised within the documents in respect of which the hon. member has asked for production. They could set to one side those which they feel should not be made available at this time because of the security practices which are involved. With regard to the others, they could provide the documents themselves or a very carefully detailed analysis, so that those people who may be involved will know precisely what they will be called upon to contend with if there should be an occasion
Motions for Papers
for a government employee to meet with this appeal tribunal.
After all, Mr. Speaker, I think that nothing less than that would be worthy of the judicial system which has reached its flower in this country. One of the proudest boasts, I think, of our democratic system is the judicial function. I repeat there will be a judicial function which this committee, even though it is termed an administrative committee, will be exercising because it will be reviewing a decision already made. I see no reason why, under those conditions, the details and circumstances under which this review will be made should not be made available so that this house would be able to assess and evaluate the sufficiency of these directives. Then, an individual whose position might be in danger may, at the appropriate time, have an opportunity to meet the charges against him, to know the circumstances under which he will be permitted to defend himself. He could appear or be represented by counsel, knowing in advance what he will be called upon to meet. I suggest that anything less than that will not be carrying out the true spirit of the judicial system of this country.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great interest during the last two days to the manner in which this matter has been debated. I was somewhat surprised by the remarks of the hon. member who just spoke when he said that the administrative body which the Prime Minister on October 25, 1963, said would be set up would be exercising a judicial function. I do not find this to be so. I do not feel that an administrative tribunal, such as the one that has been set up, will be exercising a judicial function. The mere fact the hon. member says that because some tribunal is reviewing a person's rights or some complaint they are thereby exercising a judicial function, is not correct in my opinion.
There is no question I think, Mr. Speaker, but that everyone in this house is concerned with the rights of individuals. Every member of every party is concerned and to say that, as the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) did, one who calls himself a Liberal is more concerned, is not stating a fact.
The Liberals are less concerned.

I do not believe that because one is called a Liberal makes him more concerned about the rights of individuals than the member of any other party. Any member who believes in human justice believes in the

Motions for Papers
rights of individuals. The hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) who is interrupting should be concerned because he has been doing a great deal of work in this field.
I find that the contributions to this debate seem to be really canned speeches left over from October 25, 1963.1 could not gather from the debate that there was any complaint or allegation that the proposal set out in the Prime Minister's statement of October 25, 1963 had not been carried into effect. The complaint we have been hearing is that we are not seeing, in black and white, that these directives are, in fact, being carried out. In my opinion, this is more or less an attack on the integrity of the Prime Minister by believing the head of a government, who is really primarily responsible for the security of the country, should be saying something in this house that he has not followed through.
It has been stated by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) that the directives did go out.
That is because you have heard so much.

You may question me after I have finished.
I have been one, along with the hon. member for Greenwood, who has been quite concerned with the question of security when it deals with immigration cases. I think the investigation of an applicant who wants to become a landed immigrant is somewhat different from an investigation relating to the security of the country itself. I was quite interested in hearing the hon. member for Greenwood asking today, and I think these are his words, what good is it to tell us the new procedures if we cannot see them in black and white? I believe he went on to say this was an affront to parliament. I am one who disagrees with this completely. I think that the statement of October 25, 1963, is as full as any statement possibly could be about the new procedures that were to be incorporated.
Many of the speakers have asked, what are those procedures? Time and time again the Prime Minister, the former minister of justice and the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Justice, have put on the record what the new procedures are to be. Even the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) put on the record on July 2 what those new procedures were to be. It is very interesting to note that in his speech of July 2, with regard to the first of the new procedures, he said that meets the first objection. I gather he meant by that that this met the first objection

of the hon. member's party. Then he went on to quote the second new requirement and said:
That was the second thing we wanted. We wanted a quasi judicial board of review. We did not get a quasi judicial board of review; we got an administrative board of review made up of deputy ministers.
Then the important words are these:
We are willing to settle for that as an experiment.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member and others of his party are not prepared to follow up their words and their own assurance that they were willing to settle for this new procedure to be tried out as an experiment. As the hon. member for Peace River said, nobody is perfect in these matters, especially not those dealing with security.
Here is a new procedure set forward, and it was rightly brought forward as a result of complaints made in this house by members of the New Democratic party. I compliment them on this; but this was before October 25, 1963. To date now we have not had any more such complaints, and I hope none ever comes forward again. I also hope that they at least will follow the words of their leader when he says:
We are willing to settle for that as an experiment.
1	believe there is no logical argument to the motion we are now discussing. As it appears on the order paper it reads:
That an order of the house do issue for a copy of all government statements and directives to government departments during the past year regarding security procedures and investigations.
On July 2 the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) stated there was only one directive which went out to government departments. That was also stated in answer to the question put on the order paper by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). That question read:
1.	Has the new policy regarding security investigations promised by the Prime Minister last session been established and, if not, how long will it be before it is ready?
2.	If it has been completed and approved, have its terms been made known to the employees of the government and their associations?
3.	Will a copy of the policy and its regulations be tabled in the house?
The answer to that question was given as follows on May 25 last:
1. Yes.
2	and 3. The terms have been formally communicated to all government departments and organizations-

I would assume from that that they have been communicated to the senior officers of those departments, but I do not believe that because you communicate a new security procedure to the heads of government departments, who will be directly involved in the new procedure, this means that it should be made known to the public, or even to members of this house no matter how much we may wish to have it so.
The answer continued:
It is not customary to send directives such as this to employees or associations, nor are administrative directives normally tabled in the House of Commons.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North was not satisfied with that answer and as a result we are having this debate on his motion today.
As recorded at page 4957 of Hansard for July 2 last the Minister of Justice stated that one directive had been sent to government departments during the past year regarding security procedure and investigation. He said:
There has been only one such directive, Mr. Speaker, and after the most careful consideration the government has decided that it must, in the public interest, decline to accept the motion to provide a copy of the directive.
Let us look at the precedent, or so-called precedent or alleged precedent, put forward in this house on October 25, 1963, by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin). I may say the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Macdonald) answered that in his speech somewhat earlier, but at page 4051 of Hansard for October 25 the hon. member for Greenwood is recorded as saying:
The Prime Minister has given reasons why the government decided not to have a quasi judicial tribunal, and I acknowledge at once that the ordinary method of appeal and trial is not suitable to the determination of security cases where it is impossible to confront the person affected with all the information. But, Mr. Chairman, I know of a precedent which was adopted in wartime and which I suggest could and should have been adopted here. During the war the minister of justice, acting under the powers conferred by the War Measures Act and the defence of Canada regulations, found it necessary to intern quite a large number of individuals, sometimes on a mere suspicion.
I agree with that statement.
After public representation it was found possible to set up a tribunal, which was not a tribunal of civil servants or department heads or within the structure of government, but included, as I recall it, a member of the judiciary-
-that was the present county court judge, His Honour Judge Forsyth of Toronto-
-who was free, and bound to be free, from the necessity to consider the internal or depart-
Motions for Papers
mental matters and who was able to apply a clear judicial judgment to the problems which came before him.
In the light of reading the defence of Canada regulations and the War Measures Act, and also being informed of His Honour Judge Forsyth's statements, I can say the hon. member for Greenwood is wrong, that Judge Forsyth was not applying a judicial judgment to those appeals from people interned. The people interned were interned under section 21 of the defence of Canada regulations, and 30 days thereafter there was a formal procedure by which they could appeal their internment, by which they could come before this tribunal or administrative body, whatever you want to call it, and there they were told to a certain degree in general terms why they were interned.
They were not confronted by the person or persons who whispered some words, or informed on them, whether on sound grounds or unsound grounds-

Would the hon. member permit a question? Is the hon. member aware that under the proceedings to review internment that he is referring to, a code, as it were, a form of procedure was specifically spelled out requiring particulars to be given, and setting up the types of notice procedure and so on by which hearings were to be undertaken?
That is exactly what I stated, that there was a formal procedure by which the person interned could appeal his internment. I did not detail what the formal procedure was.

Then one further question; if in wartime security reasons were not so severe that the interned person could not be given some sort of a fair procedure for appeal, which was set out in detail, does the hon. member believe in peacetime that the many, many civil servants who may lose their jobs or reputations are not entitled to the same consideration?

I do not agree with the statement made by the hon. member for Greenwood, that in wartime there were specific details given to those people who were interned. I know to the contrary from personal experience in that regard that this was not the case. It was most difficult, if not impossible, to find out why some of these people were there, although it is known many were interned because some person or persons did not like them. We know this is a fact. I say

Motions for Papers
I feel quite concerned about this matter because they did not have proper appeals. They were not informed in detail as to why they were interned. I said they were told in general terms.
But you are not concerned now.

I say these administrative bodies were not rendering any judicial decisions. There were no cross-examinations and those interned were not confronted by the persons who lodged complaints against them. Therefore when the hon. member for Greenwood asks why a similar quasi-judicial tribunal cannot be set up in peacetime I answer that there was no quasi-judicial tribunal at that time.
What is there now?

The hon. member for Winnipeg North asks what is there now. For one who speaks so much in this house and says he reads Hansard so much, I ask him again to read the statement of the Prime Minister on October 25, 1963, and also what the former minister of justice said at that time, because in those statements it is set out in detail. His own leader set it out on July 2. Perhaps he might read Hansard again. I do not have time to do it for him now. I should like to refer to some of the words used by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) on October 25, 1963 as reported on pages 4048 and 4049:
The matter under discussion is one of the most difficult problems that faces a government today. It is understandable why the Prime Minister should have made a statement this evening as to the policy of the government, for the responsibility of national security rests primarily on the Prime Minister.
These are words with which I agree and with which many people agree. The right hon. gentleman carries on with regard to the office of prime minister by saying:
He cannot put his responsibility off on somebody else. He in his person has the custody of our survival and of our security.
I agree with those remarks. The Prime Minister of this country is responsible for the security of this country as no other person is, and as far as I am concerned, after reading the statement made by the Prime Minister on October 25 and the interjections made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) it seems to me the hon. member for Winnipeg North is not interested in what was contained in that statement; he does not believe there has been such a directive issued.
That is right.
The hon. member says "that is right". He does not believe there is such a directive.
I want to see it.
Here is a member of the House of Commons who does not believe that the man who is responsible for the security of this nation-
I just want to see it.
Well, you cannot change the minds of those who do not wish to have them changed. You cannot change the minds of those who are so blind-

May I ask the hon. member a question? I did not ask it earlier because it was not my intention to create the impression that this body was a judicial body. But does he not feel that despite the fact this tribunal will be composed of administrative officials, once it has been clothed with powers authorizing it to review findings or decisions which affect the rights of an individual, that it might then be considered as exercising a judicial function and should exercise that function in a judicial way?

Perhaps when I said it would not be exercising a judicial function I was speaking only in a limited sense. In a way, the hon. member is right; it is exercising a judicial function by reviewing some evidence which is before it, but the committee does not hand down a judicial judgment in a true sense because the evidence before it is not the same as evidence which would be given before a judicial tribunal. Here we have an administrative tribunal made up of deputy ministers of various government departments. They will be able to bring before them, as I understand it, the person who has been charged, and I think this should be done. I doubt very much whether he will be confronted by the person who has charged him. In this sense this is not judicial evidence. It is perhaps a play of words; we are not at odds. But my feeling is this: let us try out this new procedure. If it does not work, then surely we can devise another which does work.

The millenium in security procedures was not reached on October 25, 1963. I have a particular case in mind which was brought to my attention since this motion was put on the order paper. It involves a young man working for the Department of Transport in

my own riding, whose employment is affected at the present time. His case has been taken up by the British Columbia civil liberties association and they have had correspondence with the Minister of Transport about it. I should like to quote first of all from a letter dated May 28 sent to the Minister of Transport by Mr. William H. Deverell, executive secretary of the British Columbia civil liberties association. It says, in part:
The employee in question objects to answering certain questions relating to his in-laws-such as birthplace, birth dates, last address while living, date of death, as well as place and date of birth of his wife. Basically, the questions relate to information of which he has no personal knowledge and he feels it is an unfair requirement of holding his position that he seek Information about persons other than himself.
In reply to this letter the Minister of Transport mentioned the statement made by the Prime Minister in the house on October 25, 1963 and the statement made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau). I wish to quote from the statement by the Prime Minister as set out in this letter because I intend to refer to it later.
The granting or the denial of a security clearance is an administrative matter, one of managerial responsibility. In making a decision that an applicant or employee may not safely be given access to secret and confidential information, the head of a department or of an agency is not denying an individual a right. No person, of course has a right to see official secrets. The department head is merely exercising the judgment he is expected to apply on the basis of all the information available to him In the way that any sensible person would exercise such judgment in hiring a secretary, a cashier, a lawyer or a doctor, ensuring that such person could be trusted with his property, his private business or his physical health.
I wish to refer later to this part of the statement referring to the hiring of a secretary, a cashier, a lawyer or a doctor in private life or private business. Later, the minister in his letter, quoting the Minister of Justice, had this to say:
In the first instance, such employees are asked to provide certain basic information about themselves and about close relatives who may influence them or cause them to be influenced in a manner which would bear on their loyalty or reliability.
It seems to me that the government goes far beyond the ordinary practice followed by anyone hiring a cashier, or a doctor, or a secretary as set out in the Prime Minister's statement. It seems to me that employers are not too interested in information concerning a man's relatives. In fact, it may be illegal for them to ask for such information. However, in connection with government security
Federal-Provincial Relations procedures questions are asked about a great many relatives and this seems to presume too much upon the influence which one relative may have over another. If a man comes from a big family he might be in a very bad position. I have nine or ten live aunts and uncles as well as 26 or more first cousins. I cannot count how many second cousins, nephews, and nieces I have. Surely, the government does not need information about all these people. Last year a case was brought up by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron) involving a young man who had been released from the navy because it was thought an uncle of his had been a communist at one time. Later, it was shown there had been a case of mistaken identity. I ask the question: What if his uncle had been a communist? Is this young man to be condemned forever because of that?
May I call it six o'clock?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when this debate was adjourned at five o'clock I was criticizing the proposed changes in the federal-provincial tax sharing arrangements.
I was criticizing these changes on the ground that they were not designed to bring about greater equalization or equity but that instead the formula was being distorted in order to bring about a desired result. I think this is fully confirmed if one looks at the table which the minister placed on Hansard at page 5184. One sees for instance the changes which arose out of the November, 1963 conference and the effect they will have in the revenue of the provinces in 1964. The provinces will get an additional $87.4 million, of which the province of Quebec will get $42.5 million, or almost half. Next year, out of $106.6 million the province of Quebec will get $54.4 million, or more than one half of the total.
There are other anomalies in this distribution of revenue to the provinces. For instance, if one takes the three prairie provinces, which in terms of per capita personal income are almost identical, one finds that under this formula in the present fiscal year Manitoba gets $7.1 million, Saskatchewan $3.2 million, and Alberta $1.6 million. If you take a comparison of the two provinces which have very close to an equal per capita personal income, namely Ontario and British Columbia, you find that Ontario gets $14.4 million and British Columbia $3.9 million. In other words, Mr. Chairman, I am saying that the federal government, in trying to get a settlement at the November conference, departed from the principle of equalization and sought to rig the formula so as to help those provinces that seemed to be most in need of being pacified.
I am not suggesting for a moment that the province of Quebec is getting too much. I am suggesting that there are other provinces that are getting too little. The province of Quebec has a very serious financial problem; in fact it has two very serious financial problems. One which is not commonly recognized is that outside of the Atlantic provinces Quebec is the only province in Canada that year after year has a per capita personal income below the national average. This should be kept in mind. It might be of interest if I just gave to the committee the per capita personal income by provinces for 1962: Newfoundland, $972; Prince Edward Island,
[The Acting Speaker 
$1,009; Nova Scotia, $1,245; New Brunswick, $1,107; Quebec, $1,417; Ontario, $1,938; Manitoba, $1,696; Saskatchewan, $1,690; Alberta, $1,687; British Columbia, $1,896. The average per capita income across Canada was $1,658. So that Quebec has a financial problem; she 'is one of the provinces that is below the national average, and has been consistently year after year. But I point out that all the Atlantic provinces are also below the national average and are much further down than is the province of Quebec.

The other problem which the province of Quebec has is that this province has now launched upon a large program of social capital expenditure. Quebec has lagged behind in the supplying of schools, hospitals and other social capital programs. Now these programs are coming at a time when the costs are higher than they would have been had they been undertaken 20 years ago. Therefore I recognize that the federal government should do something to help the province of Quebec; but I am submitting that these two problems which face the province of Quebec should be dealt with first of all by having a fiscal need grant for all the provinces. We already have it in the form of the Atlantic provinces adjustment grant. I support that program; I advocated it for years before it was introduced. I think that some formula of assistance to the provinces on the basis of fiscal need should apply to any province whose per capita income is below the national average. This would help Quebec-

speechtext:
-because my recollection is that he has made a lot of statements from time to time that could not be substantiated. The point I am making, Mr. Chairman, is that the way to help Quebec is first by having a fiscal need adjustment grant which will be applicable to Quebec or any other province whose per capita income is below the national average.
The second is by the federal government's having a social capital program to help provinces who have particular need for social capital. The way not to do it is to rig the equalization formula and distort it in the manner which has been adopted. I think this has been an unfortunate action on the part of the government.
The second matter I wanted to deal with in the very limited time I have left is the proposals which are arising out of the April conference. The minister said that this proposal to give to the provinces a 2 per cent additional abatement of personal income tax in the fiscal years 1965-66 and 1966-67 came out of the April conference. Personally, Mr. Chairman, I doubt that very much. I think it came out of the federal government's desire to get a settlement on the Canada pension plan. Certainly no such proposal was put before the provincial governments at the conference in April. The significant point is that the provinces are always placed in the position of Oliver Twist: they keep asking for more and the federal government always says there isn't any more. Then when the
Federal-Provincial Relations provinces find some way of putting a pistol to the head of the federal government they find more.
Just to see how the shares in the three tax fields have grown since 1952, let me point out that at that time the formula was 10-9-50. Then it went up, as the Leader of the Opposition said. His government raised it, first to 13-10-50, and then later on to 16-10-50, with the personal income tax abatement going up one percentage point per year for four years. Now with these two additional percentage points in the last two years of the present agreement, it means it will go up to 24 per cent. There are 24 percentage points of abatement for personal income tax, 9 per cent for corporation tax and 75 per cent for succession duties. This is a tremendous increase. But every time that it has been gouged out of the federal government; the provinces almost had to resort to a form of blackmail in order to get it.
I certainly support the government in granting this additional 2 per cent abatement of personal income tax for the last two years of the agreement, but I do not think it was offered voluntarily. I think that this is the price which the federal government has paid in order to get agreement on the Canada pension plan. I do not want to indulge in recriminations; but the point I am making is that if we are going to have satisfactory federal-provincial relations, and if we are going to put this country on a sound basis, the federal government has to approach this problem, not on the basis of how little it can get away with but on the basis of how much it can do in order to help the provincial governments, and through them the municipalities, to grapple with the financial problems which confront them.
I know, Mr. Chairman, what the minister will say. He will remind us of the problems which the federal government has and that it is facing a deficit. I do not care about the deficit problems of the federal government. In the first place, as the minister himself pointed out in his budget address, there is a difference between the traditional budgetary bookkeeping and the national economic accounts. If one looks at Hansard for Monday, March 16, and at page 29 of the white paper, the minister himself tabled statistics to show the difference between the national economic account for Canada and the traditional budgetary bookkeeping. What, Mr. Chairman, do we find? We find that in 1963, particularly for the last quarter when the economy was beginning to gather momentum, whereas the

Federal-Provincial Relations traditional budgetary bookkeeping showed us a deficit of $115 million, the national economic account showed a surplus of $47 million. In other words, when the minister or anyone else takes refuge in the fact that we may have deficits, he is resorting to the old type of budgetary bookkeeping. When we look at the national economic account we realize that, as the economy gathers momentum and we increase productivity and the gross national product, these deficits will disappear.
If the minister really believes, as he has said repeatedly, that our economy is going to grow and expand, then I do not think we have to worry about deficits. I think the government can afford to be much more generous to the provinces than they have been. I think they can afford, for instance, as I suggested a few moments ago, to increase the Atlantic provinces adjustment grant. Because the Atlantic provinces are the Cinderellas of confederation and the rest of Canada has not done fairly by them.
I think that the principle of a fiscal need adjustment grant should be extended across Canada. It would apply to Quebec. It would not apply to the other provinces in a normal period. Right now, for instance, there is the threat of a drought in Saskatchewan which could extend into Manitoba. There could be years in which the per capita income of a given province might drop below national average, and if we had a fiscal adjustment grant in those years that province would have a claim on the federal treasury.

It seems to me that this is the kind of approach which would gain the support and the confidence of the provinces of Canada. Instead of sitting around a table and cutting up a small pie, haggling over how much will go to the provinces and how much will go to the federal government, we should try to think in terms of an expanding economy, of a larger pie to be divided up, and recognize that the principle of equalization must be based not on a rigged formula but on the basis of fiscal need; that those provinces which are most in need ought to get the largest share of these equalization payments. speechtext: Which one, B.C. or Saskatchewan?

speechtext:
I am talking now of British Columbia. I represent a constituency in British Columbia. But other provinces in Canada which might be affected by drought or some economic catastrophe would benefit, and from Quebec to the Atlantic ocean every one of the provinces would benefit year after year. It is only on the basis of this kind of equalization, this business of sharing one another's burden, being each other's keeper, that we are going to build the kind of co-operative federalism which has any meaning. Otherwise co-operative federalism is sheer window dressing. It is merely a matter of indulging in eulogistic phrases unless it actually means sharing with those provinces who, for one reason or another, are less fortunate than other provinces. I think that is the basis upon which federal-provincial fiscal agreements must be negotiated.
There are two other matters which I wish to touch on very briefly. First of all, I support wholeheartedly the government's decision to continue the Newfoundland transitional grant which was supposed to expire on March 31, 1967. That expiry date has been wiped out, which is as it should be. I support the decision completely. I also support the idea of entering into an agreement with any province which is supplying youth allowances by giving to such a province a 3 per cent abatement on personal income tax and then making an adjustment at the end of the year so that the province gets back what it has actually spent. I see no objection whatsoever to that and I think that in this case the federal government has worked out what ought to be a very satisfactory arrangement. If the province of Quebec is happier with that kind of arrangement than having the federal government handle youth allowances, I do not see why any of us should object. They are not getting anything to which they are not entitled and it is equitable and fair all round.
There is one other point I want to make. I have said repeatedly in the house, and I am not going to elaborate now because I may want to say something about it when the bill is before the house, that this house ought to be concerned, and I am sure it is, about the danger of stripping the federal government of the fiscal powers which it needs to combat either inflation or deflation, to maintain economic stability and to promote economic

growth and full employment. Control of fiscal policy is one of the Keynesian techniques which any government has to retain if it is going to meet the problems of economic fluctuation. As the federal government parts with some of its taxing powers it loses this control.
What is the answer? I do not think the answer is for the federal government to take back these powers from the provinces, but I think the Porter commission put its finger on this at pages 519 to 521 of its report when it said that the time had come in Canada for the federal and provincial governments to coordinate and direct their fiscal policies.
I was very glad to see that Professor K. W. Taylor, who is special adviser to the privy council office and who was formerly deputy minister of finance, had this to say when he spoke to the 17th tax conference sponsored by the Canadian tax foundation in November last in Vancouver:
The subject of my paper is the federal budgetary process, but I do want to emphasize in these prefatory remarks that the size and patterns of provincial and municipal revenues and expenditures have an important bearing on both national and regional economic development and that these levels of government should carefully appraise the economic implications of their fiscal policies both in their own interest and in the national interest.
He went on to say:
Five years ago at a federal-provincial conference Saskatchewan suggested that there should be a regular annual meeting of federal and provincial finance ministers to review economic prospects and exchange views on appropriate fiscal policies: and two years ago Mr. Gerin-Lajoie, here in Vancouver suggested regular federal-provincial consultation to co-ordinate matters of national interest and priority. I am sure we can agree that there would be considerable merit in promoting co-ordination of federal and provincial fiscal policies.
The point I want to make is just this, that we must be very careful not to so diffuse fiscal policy in this country that Canada cannot effectively cope with either an economic depression or a period of inflation. I hope the Minister of Finance is giving some thought to the possibility of annual meetings of the Minister of Finance and the provincial treasurers with the idea of co-ordinating their respective budgets so that fiscal policies will not be purely a federal matter but a federal-provincial matter. Otherwise I think that federal and provincial budgets can cancel each other out. They could bring about economic conflicts. They could have serious repercussions for our economy, and I think this is one of the steps that could be taken to make more effective and more efficient
Federal-Provincial Relations federal-provincial co-ordination in this field of fiscal relations.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the resolution before the committee tonight is one of urgent and extreme importance, important to some provinces for what it contains, important to other provinces for what it does not contain. The entire policy of the federal government regarding federal-provincial fiscal arrangements has been and continues to be disappointing. While there has been a great deal of talk with particular emphasis on cooperative federalism, the government to date has done nothing much more than to yield to the pressures of the day, particularly as they come from some of the larger provinces, and has failed completely to come to grips with the fundamental issue which must be resolved before there ever can be any solution to the federal-provincial fiscal problem.
At the very heart of the fiscal arrangements problem is the basic problem of debt, and I am speaking strictly of federal government debt and provincial government debt. At the present time the provincial and the federal governments together, not to mention the municipal and local governments, are spending approximately $1 billion more than they are able to collect from their revenue sources. It seems to me that it does not really matter how we juggle the dividing of these tax deficit problems between us because basically, the cold, hard fact remains that in the end there just is not sufficient income to meet the demands for public services at the present time. To overlook and bypass this basic problem is simply not to face up to realities.
The federal government is seemingly content to hide behind blinkers in the belief that somehow everything will turn out all right. This attitude and philosophy is preventing it from projecting any alternative solution or facing simple facts as they are. What is urgently needed in our economy today is nothing more or less than a strong position of leadership, and I am speaking particularly now of fiscal leadership, to bring in those financial policies that will let the logical expansion of our country go forward in such a way that the tremendous wealth that is ours can equitably be shared not only by governments but by Canadian citizens themselves. We simply do not have this financial and fiscal leadership at this time. This applies to the federal government's own policies and certainly applies to the policies for which it is responsible that relate to the provinces. Unless something is done to satisfy permanently
5272	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Federal-Provincial Relations the problems we face in a more satisfactory way, what I am afraid will happen is that the provinces, provincial policies and provincial needs are simply going to polarize further than they have up to now, and instead of our uniting into a stronger nation where we would have the ideal situation of what one might call co-operative federalism we are going to be fragmented still more than we are at the present time. This applies particularly to the realm of fiscal arrangements between the federal government and the provinces.
In the minister's March budget speech he forecast a deficit for the current fiscal year of some $455 million according to what he said, as found on page 5185 of Hansard, is the traditional method of accounting. I was intrigued by those words, "traditional method of accounting". I wonder what the minister actually meant. Then I go on further and I read these words in the statement he made to the house the other evening:
Obviously there must be limits beyond which the federal government cannot go without endangering its own financial position.
What does he mean by traditional bookkeeping? What does he mean by limits beyond which the federal government cannot go?
I should like at this point to pose several basic questions to the minister to which I have not been able to get satisfactory answers in the house, and I have not seen any record where the minister has given the answers in any other place. First of all, to what extent has the Bank of Canada purchased government bonds? What is the average length of time that these bonds are likely to be held before maturity or before they are sold? How many of these bonds are likely to be held until they do mature? How much money is actually paid to the Bank of Canada in interest on these bonds which the Bank of Canada holds? What portion of these charges is returned, this accruement of interest charges on government bonds held by the Bank of Canada, to the consolidated revenue fund? Based on the replies which I think it is the obligation of the minister to give us to these questions, is it not true that the volume of spending must be governed by the inflationary pressures that exist in the economy?
This leads on to another logical question that relates to the present use that is being made of the Bank of Canada so far as government bonds are concerned. I should like to hear the minister say why a branch of

the Bank of Canada in the form of a municipal development bank with low charge rates based on actual administration costs, could not be a very desirable change in his own fiscal requirements. I am sure if he can use the Bank of Canada as I have reason to believe he is using it at the present time for the purposes that he is, there is no reason at all why there could not be established as part of the Bank of Canada a municipal development bank which would meet the capital development needs of the provinces and of the municipalities. On this basis, we would be decreasing some of these fixed costs to the extent that certainly the fiscal problems that the provincial governments face at this time would be much easier than they are.
I realize that many of the expenditures which the government faces are fixed expenditures and it is almost impossible to reduce them. On the other hand, 15 per cent of our budget tax dollar is being paid today for interest charges on the national debt. If the government were not facing this tremendous drain of expenditure for this purpose, if the Bank of Canada through such a bank, shall we say, as the municipal development bank, could eliminate much of this unnecessary expenditure, and then certainly there would be more money not only for the federal government itself but also to share out with the provinces. Then, I would suggest that the facilities of the private banking system would be contracted in making such credit available. If it is true that the Bank of Canada is holding much of the national debt at the present time, the real problem then in Canada is not deficits, it is instead a matter of controlling inflation.
Now, without spending too much of the short time that is at my disposal with regard to some of these basic, fundamental changes in financial policy which could ease the overall fiscal burden, I do want to emphasize the fact that you can only make X dollars go so far. You can cut the pie in any way you want, in as many pieces as you want or with as complicated a formula as you want, but there are still only so many dollars to deal with. It is on this basis we have to face up to this very important problem.
Now, coming to this question of equalization and the chart which the minister tabled the other night when he made his remarks. It is very interesting to note when you look over how equalization affects the different provinces, that two provinces which will have no benefit whatever from this present arrangement for equalization are Alberta and

British Columbia. As I was studying this situation this afternoon, a strange thought came into my mind, at least it may seem strange to the minister, Mr. Chairman, but it is not so strange to me. The best way for him to settle the problem he faces so far as equalization is concerned, is to go out and help get a Social Credit government elected in all of the rest of the provinces, and then he would not have any problem.
Actually, what is happening-
