speechtext: That'll be the day.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
The minister says, "That'll be the day." What he is doing is penalizing certain aggressive policies which are meeting the needs of these provinces, and penalizing the people of these provinces because they have a government that is facing up on this basis. The minister is robbing from them to pay others simply because this policy of equalization is antiquated and certainly not equitable. If you carry these obvious facts through, it seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that the policy we have at the present time can at the best be seen to be something that is merely doctoring over the symptoms, instead of getting to the root cause of the disease itself.
There are four basic facts which I want to impress upon the minister tonight as far as inequality is concerned in the present fiscal arrangements as they affect some of the provinces. These points probably overlap in some instances on some of those raised by the previous speaker. Certainly, it affects in a most serious way those newer provinces which have gone forward in a more efficient and effective way in the development of their resources and their economies and at this time is placing them in a very inequitable position.
First of all, I should like to mention the question of hospitalization. In the province of Alberta, the hospitalization insurance scheme does not depend upon prepaid premiums nor is it dependant upon a sales tax which is levied for that particular purpose. Instead, the hospitalization insurance scheme uses the principle of a deterrent, where actually as they need the services the citizens themselves contribute a small amount to cover part of the cost of hospitalization. In the over-all effect, this probably produces one of the most economic and satisfactory hospitalization insurance schemes in the whole country. It works on this simple basis. When a person is admitted to hospital he pays a sum of from $1.50 to $2 for a certain
Federal-Provincial Relations number of days, beyond which the service is completely free. This initial co-insurance principle has about the same effect as the deductible clause does in an automobile insurance policy. Instead of paying the entire cost of insurance, this cost saving goes right back to the individual who uses it most and prevents a runaway so far as costs are concerned.
Now, under the present arrangement with the federal government, 25 per cent of the hospital costs are paid to the province on a per capita basis. Another 25 per cent is paid on an over-all cost basis, but in Alberta where this co-insurance is in effect and where there is, in other words, a deterrent deductible principle at work, this amount which in the past five years has amounted to something like $7 million is deducted from this cost factor, and thus federal government does not carry its share of the hospital insurance expenditures that it does in other provinces. The province of Alberta has tried to get the federal government to recognize this principle, but they refuse. They say they are in favour of a principle where hospitalization is available to everyone without any cost. Well, such a thing does not happen because you cannot get something for nothing. Somebody somewhere has to pay for it. The principle here is simple and it brings about a more satisfactory end result. Making hospital service available to everybody, which we all agree is a social responsibility today, is a fine thing but our federal government in its policies is completely unfair to the provincial government that brings such a practical policy. In other words, you are just driving yourself deeper into the net that is going one day to draw the string tight, so far as any hope of operating within our ability to pay is concerned; I think this is unfair.
Another thing that is extremely inequitable so far as government policies are concerned relates to the corporation tax charged on privately owned public utilities. One may say this is not very much because there are very few utilities left which are privately owned, but under the policies followed by this and previous governments we are simply driving our utilities into the arms of public ownership. In some places it may be necessary for this to take place, but I think we should preserve our privately owned and operated utilities wherever we can, particularly wherever they are operating efficiently and economically.

Federal-Provincial Relations
Because the federal government refuses to recognize this principle it means that citizens in provinces like Alberta, and in one or two others where there are privately owned utilities are paying a tax that citizens in other parts of Canada, where utilities are publicly owned, do not have to pay. It is true that approximately 50 per cent of this tax is refunded to the provinces. It is difficult to determine the exact amount since it is included with the tax rental payments, but in the province of Alberta it amounts to something like $9 million. At least this was true in 1962-63, although I do not have the exact figures for last year. However they were approximately the same.
The question can be asked, where do you stop such a policy? Is it to apply to all utilities or only electric utilities? Well, the principle is there. If we really believe we must preserve and reserve private enterprise wherever it will function effectively, even in the field of utilities, then we must admit that we are through these backward and inequitable policies driving ourselves into the arms of the very thing the government says it does not want. This is like paying lip service to something and at the same time backing into it.
Another inequitable situation which has arisen in the last few months, and which was brought out rather clearly in the statement of the minister the other night, relates to the question of the payment of sales tax by crown corporations to the provinces in which these crown corporations operate. Perhaps the principle is right, that crown corporations should not be exempted from paying the tax which other enterprises have to pay. That is a basically correct premise, but what about this principle as it applies at present to those provinces that do not have sales taxes? There is no sales tax in two provinces, Manitoba and Alberta, and so those governments are being placed in an inequitable position, so far as the amount of money is concerned that the government is turning back to them in comparison with the other provinces.
Perhaps to some this might not be such a strong argument for the future, but here the government, according to the statement made the other night, is going to pay this amount of money retroactive for the last two years. On this basis two provinces are being placed in a very inequitable position. It seems to me such policies are not only unfair but they cannot be condoned, and what bothers me is that the government does not seem to be

concerned. At least it shows no indication of wanting to do something about the problem.
Another factor which has already been dealt with to some extent tonight is the resource factor in tax sharing. At the present time 50 per cent of the provinces' resource income is deducted in calculating the provincial average income. How the government can justify this kind of policy is something that is very difficult to understand. Before the basis of the agreement was altered, so far as the method of equalization payments is concerned, it entitled the province of Alberta to $23.5 million last year, but the introduction of the resource factor reduced that to $3.6 million.
In this matter of natural resource income, something which is very important to consider is that it is not just the income that comes from natural resource development itself but that which comes from sale of resource capital assets. What is happening here is that those provinces which have been in the past or are presently willing to sell their natural resources away for a pittance, are today reaping the advantage of this present policy. This is certainly unfair, particularly to the western provinces, and it will be unfair to some other provinces as they undertake more resource development.
The per capita income from natural resources in the province of Ontario in the fiscal year 1962-63 amounted to something over $5. Many of the provinces to the west had a far greater per capita income than this. In fact Alberta had a $97 per capita resource income. As a result this policy is penalizing these provinces. An example which the hon. member for Timmins brought up the other night is that the processing of the ore from Timmins is planned for North Carolina in the United States. The same thing is happening with Quebec iron ore deposits. Instead of the provinces where these resources are located benefiting from the processing, we are shipping the resource material out, and then we are taking away money from those provinces which make a more practical use of their resources in order to make up the loss to the citizens of these provinces I have mentioned. To me this seems to be completely unfair and this is one aspect of the federal-provincial arrangements which must be adjusted.
Why does the federal government insist on using national resource revenues when calculating equalization payments? We have not had an answer from the minister to this

question, and I would remind him that it is basically unfair.
Coming back to the question of equalization, there are two basic principles which the government has enunciated over and over again. We have heard them in this house and we have heard them from public platforms when government ministers have spoken. The first is that the provinces must have the right to administer their own affairs, and the second is that all provinces must be treated equally.
It is one thing to pay lip service to these basic, fundamental principles; it is another to put them into practice. It is this discrepancy between what is stated to be government policy and the working out of government policy that is causing so much dissatisfaction among the provinces.
Dealing with the question of the present arrangement, so far as tax sharing is concerned I would very much like to use the balance of my time to speak about several of the basic reforms that the minister ought to be introducing in his own policies. But I do not have too much hope that he will ever bring in these reforms because I do not see any evidence of them, either in what he says or in the policies being placed before us. Instead I want to talk for a little about what might be done as far as better arrangements under the present set up are concerned in order to adjust some of the inequities I have been speaking about. The premier of the province of Alberta after studying this equalization question has made a proposition which I think would be much more fair to all the provinces. It recognizes the fact that most provincial governments, as well as the federal government, are operating at a deficit and that in the over-all picture these deficits amount to a very large sum. The alternative equalization policy proposed involves four steps. First, the government of Canada in consultation with the provincial governments would agree on acceptable national standards of services in the fields of public health, public welfare and, perhaps a little later on, in the field of education. Certainly it will not be possible in the days which are ahead to polarize activities in all these different fields into ten different compartments.
Much is being said about our responsibility in the field of health at the present time. It is not so much a question of arguing what our responsibilities are as it is of working out how these responsibilities can be discharged in the most effective fashion on a basis which the people of Canada can afford.
Federal-Provincial Relations The second step in this Alberta proposal would be to appraise the per capita cost of providing these basic services in each of the fields to which I have referred-to set up across Canada the basic standards we want in health, public welfare and those aspects of education in which the federal government may have some responsibility to assist with financially. Then it could be worked out what the anticipated cost of all these services to be on a per capita basis. Once this has been done, we come to the third stage-the creation of a joint federal-provincial fund sufficient to meet this cost. This would mean abolishing entirely the present system of federal and provincial government income tax and corporation tax as it is known today. It would mean abolishing the present federal and provincial sales taxes as they exist today. In place of the present tax arrangements a joint federal-provincial income tax would be established together with a joint federal-provincial corporation tax and a joint federal-provincial sales tax. When I say "joint" I am not implying this is something the federal government would take and then redistribute according to some plan of its own, but to save the cost of administration it would all be collected by the federal government and then divided up again on a per capita basis to meet the needs of the provinces in providing these basic welfare standards. The joint sales tax could take the form of a national retail turnover tax which, besides being simpler to operate, would avoid the inequities inherent in the present federal sales tax imposed at manufacturers' level, and the complicated^ nature of the retail sales taxes which are imposed in most provinces. Also into this fund should go all the revenue produced by succession duties. The idea is that the revenue from these three joint taxes and succession duties would be sufficient to pay on a per capita basis the agreed minimum standard of services in the fields of public health and public welfare across the whole national scene.

Thank you very much. My remaining remarks will be brief.
There may be those who will say this proposal involves a surrender of provincial rights. However, we must realize it is not

Federal-Provincial Relations good enough for us to talk about being Canadians and then, over and above that, to talk about our being maritimers or westerners or French or English. We had better lace the fact that if we are to be a nation we must accept the principle that we need a strong federal government. We can never be a nation without that. On the other hand we want to have provincial governments which can pay their way and meet their responsibilities under our constitutional responsibilities. We are reaching a point where we can no longer talk about policies compartmentalized into so many different units, destroying the very fibre which is necessary to make a nation.
A great deal has been said by some members of this house to the effect that their provinces pay more than they get back in return. Let me call attention to the example of my own province. In 1962 the federal government collected from the province of Alberta approximately $320 million. In return the provincial government received through grants, joint projects and shared programs, approximately $90 million. In other words it cost in the neighbourhood of $230 million for the citizens of Alberta to belong to Canada. Is that wrong? I do not think it is. In return for the benefits received for being part of the nation of Canada we should be happy and willing to make such a contribution. On the other hand, if we expect our citizens to adopt the attitude toward our nation which we think they should be taking as citizens, the federal government must come forward with fiscal policies which are fair to the provinces, the municipal governments and the individuals concerned. I dislike hearing words to the effect-and we hear them more and more often-that we are Quebeckers or maritimers, or English, or westerners first and Canadians second. This is not the way in which to build a nation which will survive in the years ahead.
To sum up my remarks briefly I would say, therefore, that the building of a strong Canada and the development of an effective federal government which will at the same time permit strong provincial governments to exist as well, able to bear the responsibilities allotted to them, will depend in great measure on what is done in this sphere of fiscal relations. It is not enough to continue to patch up something which has failed to work to the satisfaction of the provinces, something which is causing division across the nation, something which is unfair, something which is harming the way of life we agree Canadians should support. Indeed, in what seems at first


glance to be a harmless and innocent resolution, we have before us here a problem which will deeply affect the future and the wellbeing of our nation.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, one would be led to believe that our economic system is behaving at present like the St. Lawrence river in front of Quebec city, where the tide rises and falls beautifully. The same thing is happening today in the fiscal field.
At times we have seen the federal government seizing hold of almost all the sources of income, even at the expense of provincial rights and, at the present time, we can see that this same federal tide is gradually ebbing away from the fiscal field, making way more and more for the provincial governments.
Mr. Chairman, I think that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) was right when he said this afternoon that politics is rather thankless. Demands are made by the provinces and by the people, and when the government grants anything, they soon forget and ask for more.
Well, the Minister of Finance can expect the same thing to recur. He must be aware that Quebec will not be content with 24 per cent of personal or corporate income tax, or 75 per cent of estate taxes. Quebec will surely ask for more than it has already received. And even if the province offers no thanks, it will not be ungrateful, because those sources of income had been guaranteed by the Canadian constitution and were taken away from the province.
The provinces have jurisdiction over direct taxation, and the federal government at the time of the war, encroached upon this field and took over those sources of income. After having made what he calls arrangements with the provinces, he withdraws quietly, gradually and hesitantly, and at times does not even want to do so. The Minister of Finance can hardly expect appreciation if his predecessors decided to impinge upon provincial rights.
When the provinces claim what is constitutionally their own, it is because the constitution has been too often violated, more particularly in the taxation field. Today, we realize that there is general dissatisfaction with regard to the constitution, and people want to revise the constitution, adjusting it to modern times, and to the priority needs of a vast and many-cultured country like Canada.

Mr. Chairman, before dealing with the bill itself, I must admit that I was surprised a short while ago-and I think it is the first time I heard such a statement on his part- to hear the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) advocate a system of joint income tax together with a joint sales tax. Of course these taxes would be collected by the federal government and redistributed on a per head pro rata basis to each province. This would work in the same way, as when the father of a family gives $2, $5, $10 a week to his son, and when the boy does not do well, or misbehaves, his weekly allowance is cut off. The same thing would apply to the provinces.
What surprised me most, was to see the hon. member for Red Deer trying to have the social allowances financed by such a tax, when the Social Credit members always advocated that social allowances were not to be financed by taxation, but by new credit represented by the increase in the country's wealth, in the real wealth and resources which may exist therein.
I was listening to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas), touching lightly on the topic of debts, stating that it was a good thing to get into debt, that it was liable to develop the economy.
On the contrary, I believe that indebtedness does not help to develop the economy in a country, but brings about crises which future generations have to bear, such as economic depression, inflation, deflation and the unemployment which prevails today.
It is because previous generations got into debt that the federal government has to pay this year $1,080 million in interest only on its debt. Second, it is for that reason that there is an outflow every year of $1,200 million going to foreign countries to pay profits, dividends and interests earned because the Canadians themselves turned up their sleeves to develop their country.
That is what you get for running into debt. That is the result of getting into debt. It could perhaps be compared to a blood transfusion given on the battlefield to a soldier who, nevertheless, will need an operation. Or it could be compared to the man who just had a heart attack; if he is given a shot in the heart, he can be revived for a few minutes, but, after a short while, everything will have to be done over again. Now, old debts are the direct cause of the financial crisis we are facing today.
Federal-Provincial Relations
We borrow money to build a bridge. But when the cost of the bridge in material and labour is paid, including the fees of the engineers and architects, we still have to pay the finance controllers twice that amount in interest, while those people have not dug one shovelful of earth or sunk one nail into that bridge. Over a period of thirty years, the interest doubles the cost, after the materials and labour have already been paid for a first time. That is what is entailed by continual borrowing.
If you borrow $1,000 you have to pay back $2,000. When the people who create and control credit lend $1,000, they claim $2,000 and $3,000 in return.
In fact, Aristotle, the greatest of all Greek philosophers and perhaps the greatest of all times said that money does not reproduce itself naturally, that it does not procreate. When you borrow $1,000 from a source of credit, you should not be expected to pay back $2,000 because money does not reproduce itself naturally, it does not procreate. Money will bear fruit only when man gets into the picture to exercise his control and create new money. When a finance controller creates $1,000 to lend that amount to the government, the latter does not create another amount of $1,000 even though the total repayment will be $2,000.
I wonder how it is that a socialist such as the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam could accept that the government financing be done by private enterprise.
How does it happen that socialism, represented in this house by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, could suggest that some individuals, some large trusts, some big financial interests he denounces by his speech but supports by his suggestions, finance what should be sovereign, that is the government.
How does it come about that it is an accepted fact that some rich individuals pocket tremendous benefits-$1 billion 80 million this year only in interest-at the expense of the government? Does that mean that financial interests, those who create money, bankers have more power than the government? If the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) and the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam admit that, I think they should be ashamed of it, since they are members of a government that accepts that a few powerful individuals who have the privilege of creating money should have even more power than the government.
Mr. Chairman, we cannot accept the fact that a few individuals, enjoying extraordinary

Federal-Provincial Relations privileges, make millions of dollars at the expense of the sovereign state of Canada and of public bodies.
A few moments ago I heard the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam say that economy had to be developed. I agree that economy must be developed. But which sector of the economy?
Economy is a general term. If we wish to develop a general field, we must first of all go into its specifications. One always proceeds from the particular to the general when generalizing, because there are three fields in the economic sector: production, exchange of goods and consumption. Now which of those three fields needs to be developed and improved in order to expand the Canadian economy?
Is it production? Complaints are made because warehouses are overflowing. We deplore the fact that warehouses of co-operatives are full of butter which has to be converted into butter oil in order to be sold abroad, because there is a surplus. In Quebec, certain shoe manufacturers can only keep their employees working three or four hours daily. Why? Because they have too many shoes in stock. The same situation applies to clothing manufacturers. House builders complain that construction is decreasing. Why? Because demand is decreasing.
We can produce in quantity and in quality more than is necessary and I challenge anybody in this house to prove otherwise. We are able to produce in quantity and in quality enough to feed, lodge, dress, in brief meet all the needs of Canadians and of the people in South America. Thanks to its production potential, Canada can be at the present time the granary of the world.
If there are complaints, it is not because we do not produce enough, but because we are unable to sell our production. As a matter of fact, just go and ask farmers who leave their farms because they cannot sell their products, whether they can produce. Such is not the problem.
If, at the time of Louis XIV, somebody had told a shoemaker who used to cut the hide, to sew and polish the shoes and to sell them himself, that in 1964 two men and a machine would be able to make a hundred pairs of shoes per hour, but that the problem would be how to sell them, I think that the shoemaker of the 17 th century would have thought: they are crazy if they cannot sell the shoes. I need a great deal of time to make them, but when the time has come to sell them, there is no problem at all.
[Mr. Gregoire.l
Three hundred or 400 years ago, there was a production problem in Canada, but this is no longer the case. There is nothing wrong today in Canada with the production sector: it is in the sector of the exchange of products that there is something wrong. No means have been found to find a market for or to distribute products, in brief to channel the production to the consumers who need it. We can only do a part of the job, but not the rest.
It is somewhat like the Quebec bridge, a tourist attraction. Thirty years ago, considering the slow speed of automobiles and the fact that there were not too many on the road, the Quebec bridge did not have to be very wide. However, as the speed and the number of cars increased, we said: Automobiles should get across faster, so the bridge was widened.
The same thing can be said about our economy. On one side of the ditch you have the producer and on the other side the consumer, but the bridge connecting the two, that is the monetary system, is not wide enough for all products to go from one side to the other. There is only one solution and that is to widen the bridge between the two. But our economists have not yet realized it; they are still advocating the system of 1800, the monetary system which was in force at the time of Napoleon. They have not understood the modernization of the means of production. Science has developed automation to a point where it is creating problems-

speechtext: For a few minutes, I have been listening with great interest to the hon. member, and I am asking him whether he would be kind enough to tell me in what way his remarks, at the present time, refer to the resolution which is now before the committee and which deals with fiscal arrangements between the federal and provincial governments.

It is easy to make the connection, Mr. Chairman. The Minister of Finance claims that he will settle everything with taxes. That is why he is bringing in fiscal arrangements, in other words, that is why he is keeping taxes.
On this side we claim that taxes will settle nothing at all. That is crystal clear, Mr. Chairman. You can see for yourself at the end of the year that the amount taken out of your salary as taxes does not settle the problem. On the contrary, it makes you poorer. It is the same thing for all those who are here.
We say that taxes will not settle the problem, but another monetary system.

The Minister of Finance introduces fiscal legislation. We say to him: Look elsewhere to settle the problem. It seems to me that, by proposing another solution to the Minister of Finance, I am remaining within the limits of the subject, since I am helping him to solve his problems.
Mr. Chairman, see what is happening at the present time. We hear about fiscal arrangements between the federal and provincial governments. In other words, the Minister of Finance in Ottawa and the minister of finance in the province of Quebec or the province of Ontario will quarrel to know which one will take the largest amount out of the citizens' pockets. That is the stake.
We say: Do not go and get more, it is not the way the problem facing Canadians and Canada is going to be settled but rather by trying to put more money into the Canadian people's pockets so that they may buy what is produced in Canada.
It is simple, Mr. Chairman, and I believe that my remarks were related to the subject matter of the resolution.
Mr. Chairman, what is the result of levying taxes? The purchasing power of the people is further reduced, they cannot buy the Canadian production, which triggers an economic crisis. Instead of levying further taxes, let us expand our monetary system in accordance with our capabilities and the wealth of our country. Then, we shall be able to put an end to the crises confronting us.
We seem to overlook one thing, and that is that taxes make one poorer, while debt-free credit makes one richer.
A while ago, I heard the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam expounding an idea dear to the heart of the Minister of Finance -they must have studied their economic system at the same school-when he said: the central government must control taxation to be in a position to deal with major inflation and deflation crises. Well, Mr. Chairman, I maintain that taxes have never brought about inflation or deflation, that is to say, they never succeeded in controlling or providing a cure for inflation or deflation. On the contrary, they brought about inflation, the devaluation of the dollar, and deflation, by increasing prices.
When the Minister of Finance imposed a new 11 per cent tax on building materials, we saw building costs rise, at least as regards the purchase of materials, by 11 per cent. Therefore, prices have gone up and this is called inflation.
Federal-Provincial Relations
Who caused inflation in that case? It is not Social Crediters, because they did not impose any taxes, but rather the Minister of Finance. Afterwards, the Minister of Finance and the Minister without Portfolio, who is not here tonight, cry out: Social Credit means inflation. They are the ones who bring about inflation, however, by increasing prices with their taxes.
At the present time, 46 cents out of every dollar spent or earned represent taxes, that is the total of federal, provincial, municipal and school board taxes. This means that prices are increased by 46 per cent because of taxes.
That is what we call inflation, Mr. Chairman. Yet, there are those who claim that by controlling taxes you can control inflation. That is not so; it is only if you control the fiscal system and reduce taxes that you can cause prices to go down. Taxes boost prices and devaluate the currency.
Mr. Chairman, there should be no more quarrels in Canada as to who should get the largest share of taxes; instead, we should strive to set up a new monetary system which would make more sense, be more logical and be based on the realities, the potential and the wealth of the country. When Canada has such a monetary system, that is a system which takes into account not only figures but also the realities, the potential and the natural resources of the country, it will be able to face any crisis.
We never had any genuine depressions in Canada. The 1929-39 and the 1957-58 depressions were not genuine. They were intended by man and by finance, and they were borne by the government, because our governments did not know better.
There was no shortage of goods; potatoes were still growing in fields, industries were operating, means of transport were still existing and developing; businesses were going on more numerous than ever; labour was more abundant than ever; there was no shortage of means of production, of transportation, of sale or of publicity. There was only one single depression: The depression of purchasing power.
Canadians were ready to work in industries to produce the necessary goods but, at the same time, they could not buy their products. Such was the depression which we had, a depression intended by man to make purchasing power scarce in spite of an abundance of goods and wealth.
To be rational, a monetary system should be able to meet all the country's require-

Federal-Provincial Relations ments and develop all its possibilities, without our having to call upon the monetary system of other countries.
We should have in Canada a monetary system capable of satisfying all Canadian needs, without being obliged to ask for credit from other countries.
Instead of raising taxes, of quarrelling over who is going to tax more than the other, instead of increasing taxes, we should see to it that consumers have enough purchasing power to buy what is being produced. That is simple, is it not?

Mr. Chairman, I always enjoy listening to the hon. member for Lapointe because it offers an exercise in seeing just where he might be relevant. Tonight I think he mentioned the name of the Leader of the Opposition, the name of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, the hon. member for Red Deer and the Minister of Finance, but not once did he refer to the resolution or its contents. The resolution which is before us tonight is much like an iceberg, but I do not know that the Minister of Finance has that much sang-froid. If you look at the resolution on the order paper it is a simple thing but one which certainly covers much more than is indicated on the surface. We found this to our surprise the other night.
I was particularly interested in seeing the casual attitude the government adopted in putting this resolution in the order of business that had to be dealt with on the basis of urgency before a certain time. At that time the government did not disclose just how much this resolution covered. Certainly this is not in keeping with the urgency of business, when we realize that this afternoon it was disclosed the other house will


not be called together until July 15. I should like to underline the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre when he was referring to the great concern of the Minister of National Defence about the passage of a certain bill on Monday night, and then we find it will not even come up for consideration in the other place for nine days. I believe, therefore, we must look at this matter with some care.
When the minister began his remarks the other night he came rather close to launching himself as he did on his first budget, but fortunately the hon. member for Ontario brought him back down to earth. The minister mentioned that there was closer consultation in the past year with the provinces, and I would say to him there was closer consultation with the provinces whether or not the government wanted it. We recall the rather hurried conference with the provinces with regard to the municipal loan fund that ran into a blank wall last autumn. Then we have the Canada pension plan, the first version, discussed in November when other matters were discussed with the provinces. This conference was resumed on March 31. Then we had that famous or infamous rump conference, when we understand that some ministers were going in by one door and others were going out by the back door, the one party not knowing the other party had been there before them.
This resolution covers at least seven items. The first is an increase by 25 per cent in the share of the estate tax. This was the result of the conference on November 26 last. Then there is an increase in the abatement on personal income tax by 2 per cent each year for the fiscal years 1965-66 and 1966-67, bringing the new formula up to 24-9-75. Now the equalization is to take into account this abatement, but as the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam indicated this afternoon we would like to know from the Minister of Finance why the 25 per cent increase in the estate tax is not included in the equalization computation.
Then the third item was the one year option for determination of equalization rental applicable in the provinces of Saskatchewan, Manitoba and British Columbia for the years 1957 to 1961-62. This is giving statutory enactment to a practice that has been in existence. Then there is the item dealing with what this administration considers to be the legal interpretation of term 29 of the terms of union with Newfoundland. The former minister of finance announced

that the sum of $8 million would be payable to the end of 1967, that it was a terminable provision. This present administration could do nothing else but satisfy the protestations and the stand taken by the Minister of Transport when he was in opposition. Otherwise it would have been a complete reversal in thinking. I do not believe this government felt it could reverse itself once more because it has done so much of this in the last 15 months. Then the fifth item concerns provincial taxes that have been payable by crown corporations, and there is a payment to be made in lieu of two years collection of taxes by the provinces under this particular provision. I think this is quite fair. In making this provision for the provinces to gain these funds there certainly was a commitment by the previous administration. However, as the hon. member for Red Deer indicated tonight, it still does not remove the sort of odd position that the provinces of Alberta and Manitoba find themselves in, since they have no sales tax.
The sixth item is a 3 per cent abatement of personal income tax in connection with youth allowances, and the seventh is the equalization payments up to the level of the top two provinces, subject to the natural resource revenue deduction.
I thought the minister made a rather plaintive justification of his stand with regard to deficits, and it is very interesting to see him take this position. If we go back over a few years, we had a continuous litany of criticism from his colleagues when they were in opposition, concerning the deficits incurred by the previous administration. This afternoon the Leader of the Opposition indicated quite clearly how those deficits came about, and if it had not been for the greatly increased payments to the provinces, whether by outright grants or conditional grants, there could easily not have been any deficits. The Leader of the Opposition referred to these payments, but I would particularly refer to one item, the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act.
In 1957 when the Conservatives took over, this act was on the statute books, but frankly it was a dead horse. There was a provision, if t recall aright, that before the scheme could become operative six provinces, or a combination of provinces having a majority of the population of Canada, had to sign agreements with the government of Canada. We know what the result was. Certainly the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who had been the former minister of national health 20220-335
Federal-Provincial Relations and welfare, could readily see his greatly vaunted piece of legislation was going to remain inactive on the statute books unless certain changes were made.
Those changes were made and soon we had agreements with all the provinces. Today the cost to the crown of Canada under that act is approaching the $400 million mark, and this is something that is not recognized by a lot of those people who comment on federal deficits, and what the administration of this part of government means.
I fully realize and agree with the Minister of Finance on the limited scope he has in dealing with deficits. Now he has recognized, by the action he and his government have taken, that there will be deficits, and that each time there is an increase in payments to the provinces the deficits are going to mount and mount. There is no magical way out of it. Certainly the growth in the gross national product on a standard taxation scale is not going to take care not only of the deficit that has been incurred but also of every future occasion on which the Minister of Finance may be forced to give way more and more.
The Minister of Finance has recognized this principle and therefore put to naught all of the criticisms mouthed by everyone on this side of the chamber in those years, criticisms that the deficits were due to maladministration by the previous government.
1	have always thought there was a great deal of hypocrisy in what was said at that time. The minister was part and parcel of that when he was over on this side and he went through that one great exhibition of voting for debt free money. The minister is going to have to increase taxes or he is going to have to go along with the principle that if he is to give more funds to the provinces he will have to shed responsibilities. He cannot get away from it if he tries for a balanced budget or a reduced deficit.
Let me now comment on the various items that appear in this resolution. I, along with the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, would like to know why the 25 per cent increase in the estate tax provision was not included in this equalization formula? I rather suspect that again this was part of the tailoring of the end product, that the government wanted to achieve a certain result and it whittled away here and there, and adjusted and patched until it got what it wanted.
So far as the second item is concerned, the
2	per cent increase in the abatement for the

Federal-Provincial Relations I am talking on behalf of all those other provinces who may be thus affected.
We get a completely disproportionate picture with Alberta, which can use these funds just as much as anybody else, and is told, "Oh, well; you have had those resources. You are developing them now, so you are going to be penalized." I think this is wholly wrong. I would like the minister in his reply on this proposal to give us a table showing the effect of the 1961 formula of the 50 per cent of the three year average of natural resources revenue, and how the present and proposed formula is and will be affecting the provinces, because I am sure there are some rather startling changes. I want to know, how does it affect British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan particularly, because I think they are the ones that are getting hurt.
I would also reiterate the remarks made by the hon. member for Red Deer with regard to the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act and the deterrent fee. I would also put in a special plea, as I have in previous years, with regard to the province of Alberta and the income tax that is levied on public utilities. I think this is a straight discrimination against a number of companies within one province and it is absolutely unfair even for a new utility to start out facing income tax in competition with a publicly owned utility that does not pay income tax.
In conclusion I would say that the Leader of the Opposition this afternoon put forward certain proposals for a complete fully-fledged conference of dominion and provincial representatives to discuss the realignment of responsibilities with regard to duties and the tax fields that must be allocated to fulfil those responsibilities. I think this is highly overdue and I would say, as did the Leader of the Opposition, that this should not be a two or three-day conference; they must be full-blown, well worked up proposals, because our biggest problems today in the relationships between the federal government and the provinces are in the economic field. So many of our ills, in those parts of the country where there is some unrest, stem from economic conditions and the other factors are merely side factors which unfortunately spill over and blur the picture.
We will be looking forward to seeing what actual legislation the minister intends to bring forward, but I would like to have, in particular, the breakdown with respect to this natural resources revenue and how it will

affect the provinces, compared with the 1961 formula.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I thank my colleagues for their kindness. I am happy to have an opportunity to say a few words in this, what has been up to now, most interesting debate; a debate of good humour, good sense and much good thought. It is a vital subject, that of fiscal relations between the provinces and the central government. I was tremendously impressed by the far reaching, very sound suggestions made by the Leader of the Opposition this afternoon in dealing with this important matter at this very important time. I think he wisely invited us to look to our history. Certainly we Canadians have never been overly interested in our history. Heaven knows, we have not glamourized it. We have seemed to avoid, until recently, very much emotionalism about any symbol of history in so far as our own background is concerned. We are far behind the United States in this regard. I suppose, I, almost instinctively would, like Pavlov's dog, salute the American flag if I ever entered an American classroom, since I was so well indoctrinated on how to regard the flag when I spent a year at school there many years ago. I think of George Washington's certain characteristics, for these too were well ingrained in those who studied in that country.
At this late hour I am not going as far as the Leader of the Opposition in any historic recital, but if we are talking about confederation we want to start at the beginning. That would bring us to the very place I have the honour to represent in this chamber, the birthplace of confederation, the city of Charlottetown, the place where the great idea was bom. I am happy that in recent years we have had some of our Canadian scholars direct their attention to this important conference, which was not fully reported through any such reportorial device as Hansard. Professors Creighton, Waite and Whitelaw have written interesting, interpretive, very fine works on this important stage in our development. It was essential in 1864 to draw together, to shake off some of the smallness of provincialism of an earlier stage. It was necessary to rise out of a sea of troubles; some of them were political troubles, some social troubles, and a great many were economic. A quotation which the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam made this afternoon was extremely

apt, when he said that when you heard a man say that he did not care for the money, it was the principle of the thing, it was really the money that he cared about.
There were long haggles in 1864 both in Charlottetown and Quebec, and in the three years between 1864 and 1867, about fiscal relations, money and the tax dollar, where it would come from and where it would go. This so-called rigid constitution of ours-I realize the British North America Act is only part of our constitution-has never been very rigid at all when it comes to financial matters. If you look at the document today you will find it is extremely different from what it was in earlier days. There have been encroachments, as they are called, by one government against another, although as was pointed out this afternoon not always has the extension of the dominion regime in the fiscal field been an encroachment. So often economic and social problems have become so vast that no level of government lower than the national one can cope with them. One thinks of what happened in the 1930's with regard to unemployment where the lower levels of government sought to deal with this blight on the life of our society.
I should like to say to the members of this committee that we in Prince Edward Island are this year very historically minded. We are celebrating the Charlottetown conference and we hope all hon. members will come and see the cradle of confederation. In fact, we have a rather ornate new cradle which has been built with direct assistance from all provincial governments and the dominion government-the fathers of confederation memorial building. We regard this as a valuable and agreeable exercise in cooperative federalism and we would like everyone to see it.
I remember in my first speech which I ventured to make in this chamber trying to lay aside the base canard that the people of Prince Edward Island in 1864 were very casual about the confederation conference. I knew that concept was wrong, and now we find the historians and archivists discovering that this was not the case at all. Indeed the fathers of confederation were well received, wined and dined; and even George Brown, who seemed to be regarded as a teetotaller in other parts of the country apparently shook off that characteristic in Prince Edward Island. The Canadians were well regarded and treated with respect.

Did they have any sillabub?
Federal-Provincial Relations

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Well, whatever it was it was bubbling. In response to this hospitality the Canadians took over the conference, and the rest is a matter of history.
But they had many difficulties then, and no federation in the world has been without them. The host province found them so difficult that they had to stay out for quite a while. New Brunswick voted itself out and then voted itself back again. Nova Scotia tried to get out before 1867. They tried very hard to get out in 1867 and sent 19 members to the House of Commons, all but one of whom pledged to come to Ottawa to take the province out of confederation. I mention this because there are some among us in Canada who believe that the stresses and strains on confederation seem to belong only to this particular era. The Nova Scotians tried again in 1886 and elected a premier who would repeal, not prohibition but confederation. But he did not do this, and 10 years later he came up here and occupied the post of minister of finance in the Laurier government. No doubt that was an improvement in his status.
Even British Columbia, reluctant to enter, was anxious to leave. The Leader of the Opposition referred today to the confederation debates, and I am delighted that the queen's printer has again printed these in a handy volume. I find that some of the speeches made then are inspiring and some are not. Apparently many of the newspapermen, as omniscient then as their successors are now, were scornful of the level of debate and critical of the lack of accomplishment in the old legislature of Canada which in 1865 discussed this great question of confederation.
In Professor Waite's volume of selections from the confederation debates he writes about the evening in which the motion was passed, and there is something so Canadian about it all. He said:
A violent snowstorm descended upon Quebec during the last days of the debate. The final day was March 10, and the debate went on into the small hours of the morning of Saturday, March 11. A vast lobby of members were waiting to vote; unable to endure any more confederation talk, they had eaten and drunk everything the house restaurant and bar could supply, and were lying about the ante-rooms and corridors of the house, impatient for the division bell.
It rang at last at 4.15 a.m., and the members crowded into the chamber. The division on the main motion was 91-33. It was a huge vote: of a house of 130 members, 124 responded-
As the Speaker left the chair members ingloriously indulged themselves in raucous cheering and singing; then, upon the early dawn of a clear,

Federal-Provincial Relations
quiet morning, they trooped wearily home to their lodgings. The convent bell across the St. Charles river was ringing five o'clock.
Yet those debates, if at times indicating that some members were less than enthusiastic, did indicate the desire to grapple realistically with the tremendous problems which united such a diverse group of people and political communities involved.
Since I started with Prince Edward Island as the historic origin of confederation I should like to come back to that province in the contemporary scene, not because it is the most important province-which it is-but because I think it represents a test case in this whole field of dominion-provincial relations. It is the smallest province. It is the one with the narrowest tax base. It has no oil, no gold, no copper and no uranium, even if you could sell uranium nowadays. The proportion of our budget which comes from dominion funds is higher than that of any other province. If I look to the statement of revenue and expenditure for the year ended March 31, 1963 I find that out of a total listing of ordinary revenue of $22,227,000, from the government of Canada comes the amount of $12,892,000. Therefore we must look to Ottawa, not primarily for spiritual leadership but for mundane and pragmatic reasons which are coldly fiscal. For many years we looked, but little saw and less received.
The story of Prince Edward Island's relations with Ottawa is a long one and one surrounded with much intensity, bitterness and immense disappointment. When the Leader of the Opposition today referred to that doughty warrior, the great premier of the 1930's, Dr. MacMillan, he very fully and fairly caught the spirit of our province. Later leaders like Mr. Matheson, the former Liberal premier, expressed themselves very candidly. As Mr. Matheson said, the St. Laurent government did not give us half a deal. There comes to every community, as often in the lives of individuals, a new era, a period of great satisfaction, a period of new opportunities. For us this came in 1957.
We who had been disappointed so long, we who had been troubled about the economic viability of our provincial communities, found that the government elected in June of 1957 moved not only with generosity but with alacrity, and in a matter of months we received through the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants funds greater than we had ever received before and increasing the total of our Ottawa contributions to unprecedented heights.


I know that the Minister of Agriculture believes that statistics are for losers and I will be very sparing in the use of statistics. But one thing which is written large in Prince Edward Island is the contrast between the figure I shall quote for 1956-57 and that for 1962-63 in unconditional and conditional grants from Ottawa to Prince Edward Island. In the year 1956-57 the figure was $5,048,000 and after six years of Conservative administration the figure was $15,035,000, an increase of 300 per cent.
What has that meant to our small province? You have only to go there to see new roads, to see new schools, and if you were one of those who lived in that province you would sense a spirit of optimism, a new feeling of possibilities engendered and fostered by a new attitude in Ottawa and furthered by one of the truly dynamic and great provincial leaders that we have in this country, Premier Shaw.
What is the situation today? I look at the figures of the present Minister of Finance and in the table on page 5184 of Hansard, a part of his interesting statement the other night, I see that out of the first $87,479,000 under the proposed changes in the equalization formula and increased tax abatement my province will receive the princely sum of $553,000. One could say that Prince Edward Island was the Cinderella at that conference, but you would get no ball out of $553,000 nowadays. Rather our province was the Oliver Twist asking for a little more.
In stage two of these new levels of largesse I note that out of $106,662,000 Prince Edward Island squeaks out $678,000. The picture does not improve as I go down the page adding subtotal to subtotal because I find that out of $264,973,000 after the April, 1964 proposals, our province receives $1,621,000. This is most disturbing. We cannot threaten. We cannot coerce by saying that you will lose all the seats in Prince Edward Island. We do not have 75 or 83 or 85 seats. We have only four. But I will say to the Minister of Finance that no matter how sophisticated his formula, whether it is achieved before or after the event, no formula will work in this country which does not have as its essential ingredient a recognition of the tax ability and fiscal needs of the provincial communities making up this country. This is the essence of cooperative federalism.
Premier Matheson was very right when he said in 1957 that the province of Prince Edward Island would disapprove of any financial

arrangement based purely on theoretical calculations designed to meet only one purpose and not the actual financial requirements of the provincial governments. I quote Premier Matheson because of what he said about the former government prior to 1957. I agree with him. He was quite right. They did not give the province half a deal, and I am sorry that the government now in office has seen fit in this instance to revert to the former bad practices.
It is not at all a new thought that the country cannot be strong, cannot be prosperous, if there are parts of it suffering grevious inequalities, unable to provide services for their people at a level comparable to that of other regions in the country. As the late Mr. Norman McLeod Rogers once said, "A federation defeats its primary purpose if through its constitutional arrangements or through policies instituted by the national government it accomplishes the gradual debilitation of one or more of the provincial comunities of which it is composed". Unless some injection of a recognition of fiscal need and fiscal ability is brought to bear, I say to the Minister of Finance that the province of Prince Edward Island will be in a very precarious position. It is my duty to present this case to him and it is his responsibility to make provision for the weakest and the smallest in confederation, his fancy formulae to the contrary notwithstanding.
This is a principle which was well recognized not only in utterances but in action by the government which preceded the government across the way. The then prime minister, the present Leader of the Opposition, opened the dominion-provincial conference in November, 1957. Apparently November was not such a bad month that year although it was a pretty rough one last year. At that time he said:
We believe that this federation cannot thrive in a climate of glaring disparities in levels and standards of service and development as between the several provinces from Newfoundland to British Columbia.
He said that; he believed that. He and his government acted upon it, and not only the Atlantic provinces went forward but no single province suffered as a result of new justice to the Atlantic region and to the other have-not provinces. This is leadership. This is cooperative federalism. This is the kind of responsible leadership we seek, that we call for. We cannot threaten. We can appeal for justice. We can appeal for a special look at the province of Prince Edward Island and
Business of the House at the Atlantic region generally. It seems to me that, of all, we are the ones to suffer most in this particular dispensation. I hesitate to use any word dealing with dispensing because there was so little dispensed, but I think that grammatically it is correct. We want a recognition of the needs of our provinces. This is a great country. Someone has said that no matter how bad the government the country is going along not too badly, and for that we are thankful. I think Canada will survive. I think it will flourish. I think that in a few years time it may perhaps take an extra spurt ahead.
However, we do not want to be left behind. The maritimes did not come into confederation because they loved Ottawa. In fact, what they thought of Ottawa is well recorded by Joseph Howe. They did not come in without making a sacrifice. No federation is made without sacrifice. It is, indeed, in the realm of sacrifice that we made our contribution. From the common strength of a united, prosperous country, we ask justice, we ask consideration of our problems and we point the present government to the clear pattern of its predecessor. They do not have to go back into dusty tomes. They do not have to call in consultants from Toronto or anywhere else. They can look at the record of the former government. They will see what can be done to strengthen confederation, to strengthen this part of confederation which most needs assistance.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before 10.30 I was speaking with the minister of northern affairs, who I see is not in the house at the moment, so I must presume his parliamentary secretary has been asked to reply to the question I raised last Wednesday. I tried to ask on Wednesday what action the minister or his department was taking with regard to some 100 telegrams which had been sent to him by individuals and organizations in Whitehorse with regard to the preservation of one of the old river steamers there which is being retained as an article of national historic importance.
It might interest the minister to know that the Whitehorse chamber of commerce, through their own initiative and a committee set up thereunder, raised sqme $6,500 from the merchants and others in Whitehorse for the purpose of establishing the Robert Service park. By their own initiative, the citizens have converted this area into what is now an extremely attractive area for tourists, an ever increasingly important industry not only in Whitehorse but throughout the Yukon and elsewhere in Canada. The same group intends to devote their efforts now to restoring the steamer Klondike, if the minister and the federal government will approve the removal of it from its present site in the area which is just above the Robert Campbell bridge in Whitehorse.
The minister knows there was money in the estimates, just before the government changed, providing for the removal of these items of national historic interest, and that it is the intention eventually to establish this area as a park area in the city of Whitehorse. I believe the deputy minister has informed the Whitehorse chamber of commerce that the target date for establishing this park and the removal of the steamers is 1967, but it has been suggested by the chamber of commerce and other interested parties in city of Whitehorse that this is too late because, if the steamer were moved now by the government, in accordance with the plans made just previous to the change of government, then this

very enterprising group, who merit a lot of credit, would be able to commence work on it immediately because they have just about finished their project on the Robert Service park.
Another suggestion made is that the $6,500 they raised should be restored to them so that they will have a sort of revolving fund for working capital. The minister is aware that there is a plan and provision is made in the estimates where 50 per cent of the costs of construction of camp grounds and picnic sites is borne by the federal government and 50 per cent by the territorial government, yet these enterprising citizens raised these funds on their own and established this park. Therefore there is greater justification in providing these citizens with the revolving fund for which they ask. It will be spent next on the restoration of the streamer Klondike, which will take this burden away from the federal government, a burden to which it was committed prior to the change of government.
The evidence of the concern of the citizens of Whitehorse and the Yukon generally is very apparent in the number of telegrams that have been forwarded to the minister and his officials. I would suggest that very serious and favourable consideration be given to the request that has been made of the minister, and that he might be in a position this evening to advise the people of Whitehorse and the Yukon generally, through the medium of his answer to my question, that he will be acting upon it soon, and acting upon it favourably.

We have constant correspondence with the Yukon on a number of subjects. I know that the hon. member for Yukon represents a resourceful people. I know they would want to arrange a method whereby they could share the cost of the proposed territorial park with the federal government and thereby the people of Canada as a whole.
This government, as was the case with the former administration, is willing and anxious to restore that boat. Mr. Speaker, yesterday, Wednesday July 8, the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) directed the following question to the government:
-whether the government intends to introduce, during the first part of the session, in case we have a vacation, legislation to reduce the cost of feed grains for eastern farmers, in view of the fact that Quebec's agriculture is going to the dogs?
The Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve) replied to this question, as can be seen on page 5206 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, you might allow me to reply and say that we are now considering the matter. I think that next week, we will probably be in a position to announce a decision concerning the payment of trucking charges for feed grains, for all farmers in eastern Canada.

In that connection, I directed the following question to the Minister of Forestry:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a supplementary question to the Minister of Forestry. Can he tell the house whether the studies in progress at present include the suggestion made by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and the Catholic farmers union, regarding the setting up of a feed grain agency for eastern Canada?
Mr. Speaker, this government has been in office for 15 months already. Last year, on this side of the house, with the support of the agricultural organizations in the country, we called for the establishment of a feed grain agency for eastern Canada.
The government agreed that the agricultural committee would meet to consider this question. The committee sat until December 1963, on the understanding that it would resume its proceedings the moment the present session started.
Today is July 9, 1964, and the proceedings of the committee on agriculture, as regards feed grain, have not yet resumed. That is why I asked the Minister of Forestry, who is now responsible for the feed grain policy in eastern Canada, whether the current survey concerned the establishment of that agency, as requested for so long by the farmers and the agricultural organizations, as well as by several members of the house.
I would therefore appreciate it if the Minister of Forestry would tell the house, and also the farmers in eastern Canada, what progress has been made with that survey and whether the present government intends to set up, as suggested, a feed grain agency for eastern Canada.

Mr. Speaker, on August 22, 1963, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) announced that from October 15, 1963 to April 15, 1964, the government would pay accumulated storage charges with regard to western grain stored in authorized elevators in eastern Canada. This was the first concrete step to help eastern farmers with regard to feed grains.
At the beginning of last year's session, the committee on agriculture devoted several sittings to the problem of feed grains and, at the time of the adjournment, it was asked that the problem be again referred to the committee.
On June 24, the house passed a motion to refer to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization matters relating to the prices of feed grains.
Because the committee showed a great interest in the study of the problem concerning

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion the setting up of a feed grain agency, we thought that it would be wise that it should carry on with that work and that study in order to submit its recommendations as soon as possible.
I do not think that any legislation will be announced before the house adjourns for the summer recess since the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) has already explained clearly the government legislative program before resuming the flag debate. However, I said in the house yesterday that I thought it would be possible, probably next week, to announce a new policy regarding the payment of transportation costs, by truck, of feed grain to all parts of the eastern Canadian provinces as well as those of British Columbia.
It is well known that feed grains are delivered to ports along the St. Lawrence and the Atlantic and are shipped afterwards by railway cars. Now, I think that I will be in a position to announce that this grain may be shipped by trucks which will be subsidized to standardize the cost of feed grains everywhere in eastern Canada.
It will be an extremely interesting piece of legislation made possible by the civil service commission's appointment of Mr. Benoit Lavigne to the position of administrator of assistance to feed grain transportation, within the Department of Forestry, which was made public on June 13.
As the house knows, on March 5 I was entrusted with the application of that policy and I immediately asked the civil service commission to appoint a director. Since his appointment was announced on June 13, Mr. Lavigne, an economist in agricultural science from Wisconsin University, has been working for us in Ottawa where he has already prepared a brief and an order in council concerning the payment of trucking costs.

Mr. Speaker, I should also like to quote some extracts from another brief which was presented to the federal government:
Custom duties. These duties are applicable to imported tobacco bought mainly from the United States and Cuba. They are 12j cents per pound for unstemmed leaves and 20 cents for stemmed leaves, that is leaves without the middle rib.
It should be noted here that there is a trend towards a gradual decrease in tariffs, as shown in the following table:

Mr. Speaker, it is high time that at the next GATT meeting in Geneva, the Minister of Trade and Commerce should stress the precarious position of our cigar tobacco growers in the province of Quebec, so as to obtain a tariff increase against this kind of tobacco, which we are able to produce in Canada. Indeed, I think we might be well advised to increase the tariff to 40 cents a pound, in order to protect cigar tobacco growers whose contribution to the Canadian economy is quite substantial. Moreover, the cigar industry is pouring millions of dollars, not only in salaries, but in taxes into the coffers of the governments, federal and provincial.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, despite the eloquence of the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Mont-calm, and the depth of the arguments to support his case, it nevertheless remains that there are still many obscure spots in the picture he painted for us.
We may wonder, for instance, whether the problem he pointed out is new, or how long it has been with us? Is there an endemic or epidemic over production in his riding? One can also wonder if representations have been made. He mentioned one or two, but we would like to know to whom they were made.
I am also told that in the hon. member's riding, cigar tobacco is usually bought from the St. Jacques co-operative by Canadian manufacturers and that growers are normally satisfied to produce the quantity required by those manufacturers.
One may wonder then what could have happened. Those are matters, Mr. Speaker, that I shall be only too glad to discuss with the hon. member.

The hon. member suggests an increase in the customs tariff. I need not remind him that this is a Conservative answer. I need not remind him either-at least according to my information-that the problem existed already when the Conservative government was in office.

speechtext:
There was no surplus? Those circumstances are rather unusual.
Anyhow, if there is an injustice the hon. member will have to bring it to the attention of the Robertson committee, which is responsible for investigating these problems in order to work out a Canadian policy for the Geneva conference.
That being said, Mr. Speaker, the department is ready to help tobacco growers. I shall personally see the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm and we shall invite the president of the co-operative to meet the experts of the department.
For constitutional reasons cherished by the hon. member, I do not think that we may discuss the possibility of selling in the province of Quebec, since it would be an interference in a field of provincial responsibility, but it is possible to consider the situation as far as exports are concerned.
